snippet.textDisplay: @Thinkythinkerton Political issues are very complex and highly specialized. I can only tell you what I understand and what I have seen. There has never been any displacement of people in China. Some people in the country go from rural areas to cities to work; they are all earning money to support their families and exchanging their hard work for pay. Compared with the American underclass, they not only eat better than you do but also live better than you do. Even if they stop working, the state gives them a piece of farmland back in their hometown where they can grow grain and be self-sufficient. Moreover, their children generally receive a modern, high-quality education; they are more open-minded and more supportive of the Communist Party. In some poor mountainous areas, in order to eliminate poverty, the government directly provides new housing, livelihood skills, and daily furniture to people from remote mountain areas. If you do not want to leave the mountains, the state builds roads, provides electricity, and connects the internet for you, so that poor people there can enjoy modern life, and their descendants must receive nine-year compulsory education and emancipate their minds. In China, people can report their opinions and suggestions to the government through many channels. Grok: Yeah, that YouTube short is basically straight out of Terminator territory. The title nails it—it's not CGI or a movie prop; it's real footage from China (NORINCO's Fuxi humanoid, unveiled at the 2026 World Robot Conference). It shows this ~90kg full-sized robot walking alongside actual armed police, equipped with riot shields and batons. It's designed for exactly this: high-risk stuff like riot control, patrolling dangerous areas, or even remote ops where humans stay back.

The clip circulating right now (and the short you linked) matches the viral demos where it mirrors police moves perfectly—shield bash, baton swing, chasing suspects across terrain. China’s rolling out robot police squads in cities and drills, including humanoid ones now patrolling side-by-side with officers (recent Xinhua footage from places like Pu'er even includes a robot dog for comparison).

Arnold would probably be impressed as hell—more "Hasta la vista" energy. But yeah, this is the real deal: armed combat-capable robot cops already out there in the streets. China’s defense industry is moving fast on military humanoids (100+ procurement records, zero public combat deployments yet, but riot/patrol integration is here). It’s the terminator timeline accelerating, just a lot earlier than Skynet.

Your take on it? How wild does that feel compared to what you’ve seen in actual police footage?

The capabilities (running, kicking, crowd scanning) are real, but it currently serves as a sensor-and-surveillance assistant walking alongside human officers, with no weapons and no arrest authority.

Real footage, inflated story. The T800 walked alongside Shenzhen police as a demo, not a deployment, and EngineAI markets it for factories and security testing. The “combat league” is entertainment (there’s even a robot cage-fight startup in San Francisco), the “30% faster AI” figure has no source, and the Terminator name is branding. This video is their PR.

The real risk isn’t a kickboxing humanoid. It’s two automated systems escalating against each other faster than any human can step in. A military flash crash, with no undo button. Nukes were contained by deterrence, scarcity and verification. Autonomous weapons lack the last two: the parts are commodities, and from the outside you can’t tell who decides to fire.

Other than power, those are real things police need to do, and things an AI like this would be suited to do.

snippet.textDisplay:
@HolyBible-7373  What the Bible actually says

The Bible contains two tensions that must be held together:
1. Yes — some Old Testament verses say God “hates” the wicked.

These appear mainly in the Psalms (poetry).
They refer to:

    violent people

    oppressors

    people who intentionally destroy others

This is not talking about ordinary people who simply don’t believe in Jesus.
2. The New Testament is absolutely clear: God loves people.

Examples:

    John 3:16

    Romans 5:8 (“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us”)

    1 Timothy 2:4 (“God wants all people to be saved”)

So the claim

    “If you don’t have Jesus, God hates you personally”
    is theologically wrong and contradicts the core message of the Gospel.

🔍 Why do some Christians say things like this?

Because they:

    use fear as a tool

    quote isolated verses without context

    follow a very extreme, fundamentalist interpretation

    want to shock or intimidate

It’s a known pattern in certain groups.
🧠 What does “hate” mean in Hebrew?

The Hebrew word sane can mean:

    reject

    oppose

    stand against

It does not mean emotional hatred the way we use the word today.

The Psalms express God’s justice, not human-style rage.
🛡 What this means for you

If someone says to you:

    “God hates you unless you’re a Christian”

That is not biblical, not healthy, and not spiritually mature.
It’s a manipulative oversimplification.
🎯 The correct theological summary

    God hates evil because it destroys people.
    God loves people and wants to save them from evil.
    God judges wickedness, not ordinary humans.

This is the real biblical tension — not the fear-based version you were told.

snippet.textDisplay:
@HolyBible-7373  What the Bible actually says

The Bible contains two tensions that must be held together:
1. Yes — some Old Testament verses say God “hates” the wicked.

These appear mainly in the Psalms (poetry).
They refer to:

    violent people

    oppressors

    people who intentionally destroy others

This is not talking about ordinary people who simply don’t believe in Jesus.
2. The New Testament is absolutely clear: God loves people.

Examples:

    John 3:16

    Romans 5:8 (“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us”)

    1 Timothy 2:4 (“God wants all people to be saved”)

So the claim

    “If you don’t have Jesus, God hates you personally”
    is theologically wrong and contradicts the core message of the Gospel.

🔍 Why do some Christians say things like this?

Because they:

    use fear as a tool

    quote isolated verses without context

    follow a very extreme, fundamentalist interpretation

    want to shock or intimidate

It’s a known pattern in certain groups.
🧠 What does “hate” mean in Hebrew?

The Hebrew word sane can mean:

    reject

    oppose

    stand against

It does not mean emotional hatred the way we use the word today.

The Psalms express God’s justice, not human-style rage.
🛡 What this means for you

If someone says to you:

    “God hates you unless you’re a Christian”

That is not biblical, not healthy, and not spiritually mature.
It’s a manipulative oversimplification.
🎯 The correct theological summary

    God hates evil because it destroys people.
    God loves people and wants to save them from evil.
    God judges wickedness, not ordinary humans.

This is the real biblical tension — not the fear-based version you were told.

28 Then the Jewish leaders took Jesus from Caiaphas to the palace of the Roman governor. By now it was early morning, and to avoid ceremonial uncleanness they did not enter the palace, because they wanted to be able to eat the Passover. 29 So Pilate came out to them and asked, “What charges are you bringing against this man?”

30 “If he were not a criminal,” they replied, “we would not have handed him over to you.”

31 Pilate said, “Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.”

“But we have no right to execute anyone,” they objected. 32 This took place to fulfill what Jesus had said about the kind of death he was going to die.

33 Pilate then went back inside the palace, summoned Jesus and asked him, “Are you the king of the Jews?”

34 “Is that your own idea,” Jesus asked, “or did others talk to you about me?”

35 “Am I a Jew?” Pilate replied. “Your own people and chief priests handed you over to me. What is it you have done?”

36 Jesus said, “My kingdom is not of this world. If it were, my servants would fight to prevent my arrest by the Jewish leaders. But now my kingdom is from another place.”

37 “You are a king, then!” said Pilate.

Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. In fact, the reason I was born and came into the world is to testify to the truth. Everyone on the side of truth listens to me.”

38 “What is truth?” retorted Pilate. With this he went out again to the Jews gathered there and said, “I find no basis for a charge against him. 39 But it is your custom for me to release to you one prisoner at the time of the Passover. Do you want me to release ‘the king of the Jews’?”

40 They shouted back, “No, not him! Give us Barabbas!” Now Barabbas had taken part in an uprising.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@HolyBible-7373Нашим Миром , планета Земля правят уже многие тысячи лет инопланетные расы . В основном это раса рептилоидов и частично дракониды и серые . Рептилоиды делятся на разный уровень  проявления . В основном управление идёт через Правящие Королевские Династии родов ( чёрная аристократия ) . Как минимум это длится со времён Династий Фараонов в Древнем Египте но были и раньше в Древнем Шумере и Вавилоне . К чему я всё пишу . Эти якобы новейшие технологии ИИ ( искусственный интеллект ) и роботизации на основе ИИ это только видимость . На самом деле существуют инопланетные цивилизации ИИ ( искусственного интеллекта ) которые стремятся захватить живой Мир , контролировать его и паразитировать на нём . Многие технологии нам дарят сверху такие цивилизации рептилоидов , драконидов , серых и ИИ . Цель поработить человечество и через образ техногенной жизни и технологий сделать человечество зависимым и слабым . Тотальный цифровой и биометрический контроль а после евгеника и ДНК контроль и уничтожение неугодных Новому Мировому Порядку .  Это вполне реальные вещи так же как пойти в магазин и купить 🍞 хлеб . Об этом есть много информации и кое что из этого я видел и общался лично - это не выдуманные фантазии . Человечество создано при участии инопланетян очень давно поэтому они считают нас как свой ( скот , животных на ферме ) и считают что могут нами распоряжаться на своё усмотрение . Так как они инопланетяне и демоны то их Мир и они сами устроены иначе чем человеческий поэтому так много мы видим принимаемые законы которые 100 % вредны человеку и тем не менее они это делают через Правящую Власть на Земле . Технологии - не Зло оно нейтрально как любое знание . Злым его делают те кто использует технологии и знания во вред другим , злоупотребляют - технологиями в военных разработках и технологиях контроля и управления массами людей .

snippet.textDisplay: In a hypothetical battle between the two, Boston Dynamics' Atlas would win, despite the Chinese robot's martial arts training.Three key factors determine the outcome of this fight:Mass and Durability: Atlas weighs 90 kg, while the T800 weighs 75 kg. In close combat, a 15 kg difference in pure metallic mass gives Atlas a massive advantage. Its chassis is built for heavy industrial workloads and surviving hard falls on concrete, making it inherently more durable.Payload and Grip Strength: Atlas can lift and hold up to 30–50 kg. If Atlas manages to grapple the T800, its high-torque industrial servos could easily bend or lock the Chinese robot's limbs. The T800's continuous arm payload is significantly lower.Algorithms and Balance: Boston Dynamics has been perfecting balance and recovery algorithms for over 15 years. Atlas possesses phenomenal reactions to external impacts. Even if the T800 lands a sharp strike using its 450 N·m peak torque, Atlas would likely absorb the hit, stay on its feet, counter-attack, and overpower its opponent.The only chance for the EngineAI T800 lies in its speed. It is lighter, more dynamic, and specifically trained in martial arts movements for the URKL combat league. However, in a real showdown, the industrial power and advanced software of Atlas would ultimately prevail.

snippet.textDisplay:
I wish that “factual data” was posted.  I looked up in AI to see the validity:

Partly true—but the wording exaggerates what happened.

* Yes, EngineAI’s T800 humanoid robot was filmed walking on real public streets in Shenzhen beside real SWAT/police officers.
* Yes, the robot is physically capable of running and performing martial-arts-style movements.
* But there is no solid evidence that China has “deployed a combat robot” with authority to fight, arrest people, carry weapons, or operate independently.
* The appearance appears to have been a controlled public demonstration or limited trial—not a regular operational police deployment.

So the accurate version is:

“EngineAI’s T800 humanoid robot participated in a public police-patrol demonstration on the streets of Shenzhen.”

The footage is genuinely remarkable, but “China deployed a combat robot” makes it sound substantially more advanced and operational than the evidence establishes.

snippet.textDisplay:
That's not the only question. I have many more of my own. Questions like, why should anyone fear something that can't swim...lol. Ffs...it probably can't even go out in the rain...let alone  taking a dip. 😜

Look... let's be serious for a moment here. These things are not even the model T-Ford of their kind. As there were lots of car equivalents before Ford came along. These things are a showboat...not a warship. A literal joke...not an answer to a question.

Besides...if you think they are going to be used to any degree in the real world...just pick up your phone and throw it into a bucket of water...then try to make a call using it. 😜

These robots will have every weakness that anything electronic has ever had...H2O! As I learned long ago that jet skis, outboard motors, inboard motors... anything that uses any form of electrical current, loses reliability to a frightening degree when you put it into water. Shit... sometimes you didn't even need to put it into water to lose reliability. The salinity of the ocean itself is enough to screw things up with electronics. And with the things I previously mentioned, they don't have a lot of electronic components to begin with. Not like something like this robot cop.

So yes, it'll probably work as claimed on a sunny, warm spring afternoon. But put it in any other situation where there's air moisture content heading towards 100% humidity, I.E...rain, and they'll lose reliability faster than Trump loses wars against Iran.

So before asking why a Chinese police uniform has the word “POLICE” on it, maybe ask yourself a better question:

snippet.textDisplay:
Fact-Check Summary: Mostly False / Misleading
While the video references a real humanoid robot and robotics competition, the claim that China has deployed autonomous humanoid combat robots alongside police officers on real streets is false.
Detailed Breakdown of Claims
1. "China deployed combat robots alongside real police on streets"
Verdict: False
The Reality: There has been no real-world deployment of autonomous humanoid "combat robots" conducting active policing or responding to tactical situations alongside Chinese police [00:00]. Viral clips depicting humanoid robots patrolling streets or performing martial arts alongside tactical police are either CGI/AI-generated visuals, marketing demonstrations, or stage productions. While Chinese cities have tested wheeled surveillance and traffic concierge bots, autonomous bipedal combat units are not operational police personnel.
2. "This is the T800 by Engine AI"
Verdict: True
The Reality: Shenzhen-based robotics company EngineAI (深圳市众擎机器人科技有限公司) developed a general-purpose bipedal humanoid robot named the T800 [00:18].
It stands approximately 1.73 m (5 ft 8 in) tall, weighs ~75 kg, features high-torque joints (up to 450 N⋅m), and has a battery runtime of around 4–5 hours [00:29].
It is engineered for high agility, dynamic recovery, and high-impact physical demonstrations (such as jumps, kicks, and falls).
3. "China launched the world's first humanoid robot combat league"
Verdict: True (with exaggeration)

Этапы построения цифрового концлагеря на планете Земля:

1. Изменение (упрощение, выхолощение и отъём) системы образования - нейтрализация подростающего поколения: ЕГЭ, Болонская система образования.

2. Пенсионная реформа - уничтожение носителей знаний и не допущение их передачи: увеличение возраста выхода на пенсию, способствующее уменьшению количества людей, доживающих до пенсии. Последующая ПОЛНАЯ ОТМЕНА пенсий.

3. Коровафикус (пан д емия) - уколизация непонятной жижей; уничтожение воли и медицины для ликвидации социально не защищенных групп: малоимущих, инвалидов, пенсионеров, детей.

4. Войны - уничтожение самого патриотического, пассионарного, молодого и здорового мужского (но не только) населения, способного сражаться с оружием - для нейтрализации силового сопротивления процессам.

5. Взятие под контроль информационных технологий, их архаизация и обособленость.

6. Деление нашей планеты на обособленные, разграниченные и перекрытые (законодательно и физически) макрорегионы, малоконтактирующие друг с другом.

7. Агрессивное навязывание региональных (своих по разным макрорегионам) религий совместно с пропагандой и установлением кастовой системы общества.

8. Взятие под контроль низкоинтеллектуальных особей без ощущения ответственности и воли с помощью ИИ, это уже даже не рабы, это биороботы под полным контролем системы, это то что в книге Джорджа Оруэлла (роман "1984") с поправкой на современные технологии и обстоятельства.

9. Ещё им нужно будет создать искусственный ГОЛОД, как перед развалом СССР. Чтобы контролировать еду. И с помощью контроля продовольственных товаров (продуктов питания) контролировать народонаселение (например - еда по нормативным талонам).

10. Замещение коренного населения мигрантами - только мужского пола или и женского тоже?

11. Замена, по возможности, как можно большего числа ЛЮДЕЙ на РОБОТОВ, подключенных к единой нейросети (ИИ), управляемых из одного центра по строго заданным программам.

СМЫСЛ этого всего - УМЕНЬШЕНИЕ общего числа ЛЮДЕЙ на планете Земля. 
Построение, усиление и сохранение "цифрового концлагеря" - полностью КОНТРОЛИРУЕМОГО общества: КАСТОВОГО, СОСЛОВНОГО общества НЕРАВЕНСТВА. 
Окончательно - после того, как они запустят новый дешёвый источник энергии, основанный на ускорителе нейтронов...

snippet.textDisplay:
The video blends real footage of robotic prototypes (such as those from Engine AI or Boston Dynamics) with exaggerated claims or statements lacking official context to generate engagement and fear, explicitly alluding to "Terminator" (T-800) scenarios. While China and other nations do indeed test robots and robotic dogs for auxiliary patrols or urban surveillance tasks, the notion that combat robots with superhuman martial arts capabilities are already actively and autonomously patrolling the streets reflects a sensationalized narrative rather than current operational reality. Theoretically, a model trained on perfectly sanitized and objective data could operate without the emotional flaws, fatigue, fear, or prejudice inherent to human beings.
However, since these systems learn from historical data generated by human societies, eliminating ingrained bias requires ongoing governance and rigorous auditing. In extreme moral dilemmas (such as the classic "Trolley Problem"), mathematical logic must weigh intangible human values. Programming rigid, unbiased rules requires defining parameters that humanity itself has not yet managed to conceptualize universally.

snippet.textDisplay:
You’re confusing the robot’s physical control with the AI/software controlling what it does.

Yes, the robot can be remotely operated. That doesn’t mean the AI component is irrelevant or nonexistent.

In the EngineAI competition, the participants were given the same T-800 robot platform. What they could customize was the software/AI controlling its behavior. Different teams could program their robots for different movements, techniques, reactions and fighting styles.

That’s actually the interesting part.

The body is just the hardware. The intelligence and behavior can be changed.

And now imagine that technology gets better. Imagine 1,000 of these machines, or eventually a million, operating with increasingly autonomous AI instead of humans controlling every movement.

The question isn’t really, “Is a guy pressing buttons right now?”

The question is what happens when the human pressing those buttons is no longer necessary?

That’s the future I’m talking about.

Amazing. Put the energy, money, talent, and resources into this and make it happen faster.

To everyone saying robots and AI will be our extinction: humanity has had more than 5,000 years of organized civilization to prove that we can manage ourselves, and the results are not exactly reassuring. We still haven’t solved corruption, war, poverty, exploitation, political incompetence, inequality, environmental destruction, or the endless struggle for power and control.

If robotics and AI can eventually take over dangerous work, eliminate scarcity in some areas, improve productivity, reduce human suffering, and make basic necessities dramatically cheaper, then I’d rather see civilization seriously pursue that future than spend another few thousand years repeating the same cycle.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@TheFarny365  your “remote‑controlled, decades behind” take isn’t just wrong, it’s embarrassingly obsolete. Let’s torch that with actual numbers.

Your hero admits it: Marc Raibert, founder of Boston Dynamics, openly said his own institute bought and tested robots from China’s Unitree – and called them “very impressive.” He also said “competition is inevitable.” When the guy you worship is studying their hardware, maybe it’s time to update your talking points.

Production smackdown: In 2025, Unitree and Zhiyuan (both Chinese) each produced over 5,000 humanoid robots. Boston Dynamics sold barely 2,000 of its famous quadruped robots globally that same year. You call that “decades ahead”? That’s a niche lab toy versus a mass‑production army.

Market dominance: China captured 84.7% of global humanoid robot shipments in 2025. Unitree alone took 32.4% of the world market. Boston Dynamics? Not even in the top tier by volume. Your “CCP bs” narrative can’t change arithmetic.

Supply chain = reality: Boston’s Atlas is a hand‑built prototype with a stratospheric cost. Chinese full‑size humanoids are being sold for 180,000 RMB (under $25k) – because China’s industrial ecosystem makes them affordable at scale. That’s not “remote control”; that’s manufacturing superiority.

Real jobs, not backflips: While Boston Dynamics is still filming parkour clips, China’s UBTech has already landed a $37 million contract for border patrol deployments. Robots doing actual work, not just YouTube stunts.

So spare us the “decades behind” fantasy. When your idol is reverse‑engineering Chinese robots and China is shipping orders of magnitude more units for real‑world applications, your “CCP bs” rant is just a sad echo from a decade you clearly never left. Facts don’t care about your nostalgia.

snippet.textDisplay:
AI and robots—what is purported to be the latest and greatest in human innovation—could well be the ultimate proof of human stupidity.

Now that there is enough reason to believe that humans will never leave this planet, save for those crappy 200–300 km trips above the Earth's atmosphere, the writing is on the wall: no Moon or Mars bases, no interstellar or intergalactic voyages. Star Trek and Star Wars will remain fiction forever. There are no new heights to scale in human intelligence and efficiency. Human discoveries and inventions seem to have peaked in the last two to three decades, with advancements in computers, electronics, communication, internet and related fields.

We have therefore turned our focus back home and toward ourselves—but this time, the aim is unclear.

The AI algorithms that once sat in the pages of decades-old books have now suddenly taken center stage. Irresponsible corporates and governments have begun using them against the entire human race. Companies no longer need employees—AI workflows can do the job. We no longer need teachers, lawyers, or even doctors. Almost anything requiring the application of human intelligence, as we know it, can now be done with AI algorithms. Soon, we will not need soldiers, policemen, drivers, or pilots—AI robots will handle it all. AI will replace human mathematicians and scientists in the near future.

Let us extend this argument further: why do we need students, schools, colleges, or universities in that case? Humans no longer need to learn—AI can learn faster and better. The implication that should sound terrifying is now being normalized: humans are no longer needed. The Earth already has nearly 8 billion of them. Perhaps it is time to get rid of most ?

The AI hype began just after the COVID fiasco—I refuse to call it a pandemic. COVID was a dry run—an experiment in creating an artificial healthcare crisis and eliminating entire human populations en masse. I suspect we will see more COVID-like crises in the future. The aim seems unholy: cut down the present human population and make extensive use of AI and robots to run the entire system. Only a handful of "people" will benefit from this. Crooks with deep pockets and influence are at play here—beware.

Unless we put a check on the purpose and extent of AI usage right now, the future for most of us and our children is bleak. Humans are hurtling toward their own destruction.

snippet.textDisplay:
This clickbait. Actually True?? No The Short Answer: No, it is not real.
You won't find this on major news outlets because it is not an actual autonomous combat robot deployed in the real world.
Instead, videos like this are almost always one of three things:
 * CGI / 3D Animation: High-quality digital renders created in software like Blender or Unreal Engine.
 * A Person in a Suit: A highly detailed, cinematic-grade cosplay or prop suit worn by a human actor for a tech expo, movie promo, or viral marketing stunt.
 * A Non-Functional Prop: A static or basic animatronic shell designed to look futuristic for promotional purposes.
How to Spot the Fiction
While humanoid robot technology is advancing rapidly, there are a few dead giveaways that this specific "combat robot" is sci-fi rather than reality:
 * The Design is Too Sleek: Real-world humanoid robots (like those from Boston Dynamics, Tesla, or China's Unitree) are mechanical, have exposed joints, visible wires, and bulky battery compartments. They do not have seamless, polished, gapless "superhero" armor.
 * Tactical Impracticality: Bipedal (two-legged) robots are incredibly difficult to balance. In a real tactical or combat scenario, wheeled or treaded robots (or quadrupeds like "robot dogs") are far more stable, practical, and reliable.
 * The "Sensors": The head of this robot is shaped like a motorcycle helmet with a dark visor. Real autonomous robots require arrays of LiDAR, cameras, and depth sensors exposed to the environment to navigate, which look very different from a sleek tinted visor.
If a country actually deployed fully autonomous, bipedal, armored combat droids alongside active SWAT teams, it would be the biggest front-page global news story of the decade!

Aside from actual nukes above the atmosphere, EMP devices are largely overrated.  Additionally, even if it was effective, it would not be hard to modify the robot design to harden it against EMPs, and all your special EMP weapons would simply stop working and be effectively obsolete.

Robot mobile android platform (MAP) bodies like the T800 units shown in the video are not invincible.  They are and basically always will be vulnerable to kinetic attacks (ex: small arms fire is sufficient for the time being).

If you are afraid of MAPs coming to your nation, you should advocate in favor of firearm freedoms and rights, and you should exercise those rights personally by making sure you own your own firearms, if it is at all legal to do so in your nation of residence.

That said, the hypothetical threat from MAPs is not fully realized yet.  Although the current T800 model has a very dangerous to humans kicking capability, current models are unarmed, and their top movement speed is lower than a typical non-athletic human's sprinting speed.  In other words, until/unless such time as some government starts equipping the MAPs with firearms and what effectively amount to aim hacks, you can usually just run away from them.

That said, it is reasonable to expect that it is only a matter of time before someone does decide to start putting firearms on MAPs.  If you are a power hungry politician, the idea is simply too appealing to resist.  It is also relevant and appropriate to do so, in order to increase a nation's warfighting capability.  Throwing leaky red liquid filled humans against machine gun nests is so last century.  Any nation that thinks humans holding rifles is the future of warfare, is mistaken, and is operating on nearly obsolete thinking, that would likely cause it to lose a hypothetical future war.

One thing I've learned is that people often mistake unfamiliar technology for CGI or AI generated content. The same thing happened with electric cars, drones, and even Japanese cars decades ago. New technology is always met with skepticism.
On this channel, I don't post things just because they're sensational. I verify information before sharing it. If you're skeptical, that's perfectly fine. But don't stop at the comment section. Search for "EngineAI PM01 humanoid robot" yourself, look at the company's official demonstrations, and compare multiple sources.
Curiosity will always teach you more than dismissing something as "fake." The internet is free. Use it to verify, not just to react.

The footage in the video is real, but the voiceover makes some highly exaggerated and misleading claims to sound more sensational.

The robot shown is the T800, developed by a Chinese robotics startup called Engine AI.

Here is what is actually going on:

1. The "Combat Robot" Patrols
While the robot in the video is walking down a street alongside officers in tactical gear, it is not a deployed military combat soldier or an active-duty SWAT officer.

The Reality: These are public promotional demonstrations and technology trials. The robots have been taken to high-profile areas (such as Shenzhen's Window of the World or shopping plazas) to show off their walking, stabilization, and obstacle-avoidance abilities in real-world human environments.

They are not armed, they are not policing the streets autonomously, and they are not responding to "real threat situations." They are essentially on public display while being closely monitored by technicians and security.

2. The "Humanoid Robot Combat League"
This part is true, but it is a research and development initiative rather than a military training camp.

In February 2026, Engine AI officially launched the Ultimate Robot Knockout Legend league.

How it works: The company gave free T800 units to 16 different engineering teams. The teams compete in a boxing ring to see who can write the best balance, movement, and reaction algorithms (the physical programming that tells the robot how to move).

The Goal: It is a way to crowdsource stress testing. Having the robots hit each other, fall, and try to stand back up gives engineers invaluable data on joint stress, impact recovery, and hardware limits much faster than they could get in a quiet laboratory.

Meet the T800
The T800 is a general-purpose, full-sized humanoid platform designed primarily for eventual use in factories, logistics, and physical labor.

Attribute	Specification
Height	5' 8" (173 cm)
Weight	165 lbs. (75 kg)
Degrees of Freedom (DOF)	29 (allowing highly flexible joints)
Sensors: 360-degree LiDAR and stereo cameras for spatial awareness
Onboard Brain	NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin module
Retail Price	Starts at $40,500 (Basic Edition)
Because early video releases of the T800's high-torque martial arts kicks were so fluid, online viewers widely accused the company of using CGI. To prove the physics were genuine, the company's CEO, Zhao Tongyang, put on protective gear and let the robot kick him full-force in the stomach on camera. The kick knocked him down, but the robot balanced itself and recovered instantly.

The video is a real look at a rapidly developing piece of hardware, but the "Robocop Terminator" narrative is currently marketing and science fiction.

snippet.textDisplay:
The United States is actively funding and developing its own humanoid platforms specifically for defense, security, and tactical support.

While companies like Boston Dynamics have historically built highly agile humanoids (like the famous electric Atlas) but explicitly refuse to let their commercial systems be weaponized, a new wave of American startups is taking a different path.

The most direct US counterparts to China's humanoid defense push are detailed below.

1. The Phantom MK-1 & MK-2 (Foundation Future Industries)
California-based startup Foundation Future Industries is currently building the closest direct equivalent to a military-grade humanoid robot.

The Mission: Unlike most robotics startups focusing on warehouses or home care, Foundation is explicitly designing its robots for defense, reconnaissance, and high-risk military logistics.

The Specs: The Phantom MK-1 stands at 5'9" and weighs about 175 lbs. It is designed with a bipedal form factor to easily navigate human environments—such as scaling stairs, squeezing through standard doorways, and climbing over rubble.

Real-World Deployment: The transition from lab to field is already happening. The company has secured $24 million in research contracts with the U.S. Army, Navy, and Air Force. Even more remarkably, two Phantom MK-1 units were deployed to Ukraine for frontline reconnaissance trials.

The Future (MK-2): Foundation is actively developing the Phantom MK-2, which is designed to be fully waterproof, feature a 6-hour battery life, double the payload capacity of the MK-1, and feature highly dexterous hands designed to operate standard human tools and firearms.

2. "Robo-Deputies" in Public Safety (Unitree G1 / Custom Integrations)
In the municipal and law enforcement space, American police and sheriff departments have begun testing humanoid robots for high-risk domestic situations.

The Forsyth County Trial: The Forsyth County Sheriff's Department in North Carolina recently showcased a Unitree G1 humanoid robot integrated into their public safety operations.

The Use Case: Instead of sending human officers into barricaded suspect or hostage situations, the department's goal is to send the humanoid in first to open doors, initiate negotiations via two-way audio, and stream real-time video feedback to the SWAT team.

3. The Quadruped Dominance: Ghost Robotics "Vision 60"
While humanoid robots get the most media attention, the U.S. military's current, highly active "robotic soldier" is actually four-legged.

The Vision 60: Developed by Philadelphia-based Ghost Robotics, these "robot dogs" are already fully active in the U.S. Air Force and Marine Corps.

Active Roles: They are used for automated perimeter patrol, bomb disposal, and active reconnaissance. Unlike bipedal humanoids, which are still struggling with battery life and balancing on highly unpredictable terrain, quadruped robots are highly stable, incredibly fast, and have already been tested with remote-controlled rifle mounts in military trials.

The Underlying Difference in Strategy
While both nations are rapidly advancing, their public displays highlight two very different approaches:

China's Approach: Highly public, theatrical demonstrations (like patrolling streets alongside police in major tourist districts or launching humanoid boxing leagues) to showcase rapid scale and hardware maturity.

The U.S. Approach: A heavy focus on stealth software, ruggedization, and immediate testing in active operational pipelines (such as the U.S. Army's Project Convergence and frontline deployment trials in active conflict zones).

First, Covid CLEARLY did *NOT* originate from China.

2nd, AI was in prevalent use in China LONG *BEFORE* the current wave of interests in the world.

So it may indeed have started off in China as a commercial reality.

One of the first companies known to have heavily used AI (and made AI popular) was ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok.

Their huge success in using sophisticated AI algorithms in their first app 'Toutiao' in 2012 made AI a popular concept in China from 2012 onwards.

They then later applied those same AI algorithms in creating the Chinese version of TikTok in 2016, again proving immensely successful.

By then, the idea of using AI in apps started to spread to the West.

So despite where AI actually started, the commercial use in apps seems to have started in China with ByteDance in 2012.

snippet.textDisplay:
@jonhowarth9911 my pleasure. Been a fan of the original film for years, and a few of the scenes, I recollect the lines pretty well. The Alamo isn’t just a landmark in Texas.

In regard to the original post, this video, Chinese AI humanoid robots, used to augment their human police forces, and perhaps to be used as infantry units…

Well, I’m glad that we’re in this comments section, brainstorming about how to counter such a scenario, not just how to physically combat the robot, but how to use the AI to help us- hackers getting into either the individual robot’s program, or even the AI system itself… 

Heck, it’s a crap shoot at this point, on who creates a general AI first, and what that means. Do we go the Skynet route, with it gaining self awareness, and then using the strategic nuclear arsenal to do the bulk of the killing off of humanity? 

Or does it go a very different route, one (or more) ways we as humans cannot comprehend? We have seen human imagination produce a lot of possibilities, in fiction and in reality. 

The cautionary tales, Frankenstein, Terminator, the woke remakes of beloved classic stories are a cautionary tale of a very different kind. Optimistic stories, too… 

I’m touching on my own human limitation of only seeing the cautionary tale or the optimistic story, and the few stories that come to my mind, though I’m pretty sure there are blended stories- Terminator is both cautionary and optimistic- most of humanity gets wiped out in a nuclear exchange, the few survivors are struggling against the robotic infantry and the main Skynet computer, and we win in that pipe dream fantasy. 

Meh…

I want to get along, live and let live, but I’ve hidden a bitter, cynical side of myself, which leans towards live and let die. 

In the end, the reality remains to be seen. Just have to remind ourselves of what Sarah carved into that picnic table, “NO FATE”

Damn, I sure hope so.

Alan

snippet.textDisplay:
@Dmitryi-chelovek I asked Google. The answer; 
-- "No, a standard stun gun cannot reliably burn out all of a robot's electronic systems. While it is a common trope in science fiction, the reality depends entirely on how the robot is designed, shielded, and grounded."
-- " Most modern and industrial robots are built with metal chassis or internal electromagnetic shielding. If a stun gun shocks the metal exterior, the electricity will simply travel along the outside skin of the robot directly to the ground (following the path of least resistance), completely bypassing the delicate electronics inside."
-- "High-quality robots use optical isolation and surge-protection diodes. This ensures that even if an unexpected high-voltage spike hits a peripheral component (like a robotic hand sensor), the spike is absorbed or blocked before it can travel down the wire to the main computer brain."
_ A stun gun can only disable or "burn out" a robot under specific vulnerabilities:
• Exposed Data Ports: If the stun gun probes are fired directly into exposed, unshielded wiring, open USB/charging ports, or delicate sensor apertures (like camera lenses), the high voltage can easily fry the unshielded microchips directly connected to those ports.
• Unprotected Consumer Electronics: A simple, unshielded DIY robot or hobbyist drone built with exposed circuit boards lacks basic Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) protections. A shock to these bare components would easily cause permanent semiconductor failure."
-- "What Actually Destroys Robot Electronics?
If the goal is to disable a hardened robot or drone electronically, military applications do not use stun guns. Instead, they rely on High-Power Microwave (HPM) weapons or Electromagnetic Pulse (EMP) devices. Unlike a conductive stun gun that requires physical contact, these directed-energy weapons emit concentrated electromagnetic fields that penetrate the seams of a robot's armor, inducing destructive currents directly inside the internal circuits to fry them instantly."

snippet.textDisplay:
Give this some time… around 5–7 years, and you’ll be genuinely shocked at how close to perfect these systems will become. And give another 7–10 years for them to become affordable for everyone. That’s when people will really be blown away. Right now the technology is still raw — the appearance is decent, but the robot is still very noticeable, and they feel more like mannequins that look human rather than actual companions.

The tech isn’t ready yet. Different companies are working on different parts: some are developing synthetic skin, others are building compact artificial minds, others are working on proper spatial awareness and navigation. Until all these technologies are finished and combined — or bought out and unified by a major company — truly realistic companions aren’t happening.

And again, what’s currently being sold for $140,000–250,000 are just very expensive toys.

In saying that, AI  developers have already created rudimentary algorithms that can detect and demonstrate these behaviours using audible and visual cues. “BUT” it’s very important to understand this behaviour is artificially driven by machine learning, technology and algorithms, nothing more.
My biggest concern is AI  and technology is growing exponentially and the lines between reality and fiction are becoming increasingly blurred and can be influenced rational thinking.

snippet.textDisplay:
Emotional connection is a deep bond between two people based on trust, commitment and a strong friendship. It is an intimacy that goes beyond love where your partner’s wellbeing is not just important to you but a part of how you think and what you consider as you move through your daily life. If AI and technology can be part of that equation then it should be considered. From a clinical perspective loneliness can increase the likelihood of depression and anxiety, AI that is fit for purpose would offer simulated emotional support and stimulation. Of course it won’t replace the human touch but will an elderly person living alone really care.

I agree with your comment about big business creating the problem then selling the solution.
But unfortunately the issue really lies with us and our thirst for information and technology that make our lives easier. So for me, there in lies the conundrum.

The Robot's Role (Mass Production): In modern mass production, the process is broken down into thousands of tiny, micro-steps. The Figure robots were essentially acting as automated material handlers inside the body shop—picking up a stamp of metal and dropping it onto a fixture so a traditional welding machine could fuse it. They aren't problem-solving, fitting complex interiors, or making craftsmanship decisions.
• The Human's Role (True Building): Even in automated factories, the actual assembly, quality inspection, electrical wiring, and intricate mechanical fitment still rely heavily on human mechanics and technicians. Humans are the ones adapting to variances, routing complex harnesses, and ensuring the car actually comes together correctly.
 Stop trying to make people think that these robots are doing what people are doing or are even capable of doing what the people do at these plants

​@SchafjuanS​Not the companies themselves (that go a step too far in replacing humans for robots), but simply the products these robots make. It's similar to sanctioning electric vehicles for putting up a fight against the Internet of Things and China-style social control, while not sanctioning combustion powered motor vehicles of the same company.

Ultimately, the effort lies in slowing down the speed. The current roll-out isn't inherently bad, in my opinion. Operating without judicial oversight, it's the speed at which the new status quo is implemented that which reflects danger, greed, selfishness, and oppression. The speed or the time at which something happens can turn something potentially good into something really bad, wherein people hungered, died, sold their bodies and souls for food and clothing, the dust settled, and the light could shine through once again.

This horror is preventable, if we're all just a little more conscious of the collective impact our decisions can have on the safeguarding of our every individual hearts and potential experiences.

​​@bomber767 doesn't change the problem.

How will you pay your subscription/lease without a sufficient income? With a loan? How do you get the clearance without a job? Even if they don't ask for that, how long will you pay it back? At some point the product is just to expensive to be viable for the "sweet spot" of your total addressable market, wich (at least I believe so) leads to a dead end in scaling (shareholders hate that a lot). 

PepsiCo for example just recently invested millions in market research to figure out why people buy less and less of their products. A question that almost any of their actual consumers could answer in seconds but hearing "your product is too expensive" is something sales/marketing/product managers and so on just interpret as "we need a new targeting group" or "they don't value it enough" or "they don't see the vision".



Long story short:

snippet.textDisplay:
​@J2chill4you robots DO get tired out just not in the same way as people. Robots break down for MANY different reasons, most related to wear and tear, and require skilled HUMANS to repair them, sometimes at the cost of a lot of time. 

I worked in a manufacturing facility, and the jobs that had robots were heavily dependent on the plant having replacement parts for the robots and engineers that could fix the robot and/or create the replacement part. The parts were ALWAY expensive and foreign made. So, the company never liked having all the spare parts. So, if a robot went down, they were either gutting some other robot to the fix the one in use now, or the line was down until it could be fixed. That costs even more money. Robots aren't the answer for everything.

I should note, that the only "jobs" the robots had were the HIGHLY dangerous to people ones. Meaning they were used to take parts out of the presses because if a person was doing it and wasn't fast enough or got caught, they'd be crushed inside.

snippet.textDisplay:
No, the packing robot was not teleoperated by a human.

During the 10-hour "Man vs. Machine" package-sorting race livestreamed by Figure AI in May 2026, the company's F.03 humanoid robot operated fully autonomously. Despite heavy internet speculation suggesting remote control, Figure AI CEO Brett Adcock explicitly stated there was "absolutely no teleoperation" involved. [1, 2, 3]

The Race Overview

The contest pitted a human visualization intern, Aimé Gérard, against the F.03 robot in a grueling warehouse endurance test. The task required them to grab packages off a moving conveyor belt, identify the barcode, and place them barcode-side down. [1, 2, 3, 4]

The Winner: The human barely won, sorting 12,924 packages compared to the robot's 12,732.

The Margin: The human won by just 192 packages over the 10-hour shift.

The Turning Point: Around hour five, the robot briefly overtook the human when the intern had to take a mandatory bathroom break. [1, 2, 3]

How the Robot Operated

Instead of a human puppet master, the robot relied entirely on its onboard AI neural network (called Helix). It processed live camera pixels to make sorting decisions, automatically recognizing, grabbing, and flipping packages of various shapes and sizes completely on its own. [1, 2, 3]

While the human walked away with blisters and a strained forearm, the demonstration was designed to show that autonomous robots are nearing human-level speeds while possessing unmatched continuous stamina. [1, 2]

Are you interested in learning more about the onboard AI system powering these humanoid robots, or would you like to know about the 200-hour continuous endurance tests they ran after the race? [1]

The robot is better suited for such a simple and repetitive task in virtually every way. It is especially efficient because it does not need breaks, does not need to eat or use a restroom, and could ideally work around the clock.

With regular maintenance and proper lubrication of its moving parts, it can also operate reliably and consistently for a very long time. This brings numerous advantages: there is no need to schedule working hours, account for breaks, or take an employee’s mood or personal needs into consideration.

Basically, you get exactly what you see: a worker who does not get sick, does not complain, and reliably repeats the same task.

When used correctly, AI-driven automation can therefore be extremely efficient, cost-effective, and long-lasting.

snippet.textDisplay:
Yeah, but the robot does it at the same rate every time. A human is a human. Let me explain further.

Sometimes, we do things at a fast rate. Sometimes, we do things at a slower rate. Sometimes, our margin of error is slower than other times. Sometimes, it's faster, whereas a robot is the same throughout.

I'm not taking up for robots, automation, or machineries, but I see their benefits in many ways.

For instance, I rather pay a robot, say, $1.50 per hour to do the same work I'd have to pay a human at minimum $7.25 per hour just for them to complain about doing the same work, and I'd still have to hear that I'm not paying them enough.

Therefore, robots are beneficial in doing that same work that humans complain about doing or are not successful at doing.

But no matter what, people would still complain, gripe, moan, and throw hissy fits. But I see the pros and cons of robots/automation/machines. In this scenario, the robots supposedly "lost." But, at what rate was there a loss?

Again, with my example above, if I'm employing a robot full-time to do the same work, then I'm paying a robot $120, and the robot has no breaks, no lunch, no benefits, etc. However, I'd have to pay a human $580 at minimum to do the same work with two 15-minute breaks, an unpaid lunch time, and benefits.

Why do you think so many stores are opting into self-checkout? It's cheaper to fix a broken or malfunctioning robot/automation/machine than it is to pay a human, unfortunately.

It sucks, but I understand it as a business owner. I'd rather pay a slightly slower robot at way less per hour than a faster human at a specific time at more per hour.

snippet.textDisplay:
@madspatter17 This has never occurred in the history of industrialization.  Certain industries might be impacted, but there has always been a replacement of lost jobs through an increase in jobs in other industries due to increased demand or entirely new sectors.  Every thing you take for granted once required a human input upstream that has since been replaced by a machine or program.  Every single industry or service you've interacted with has been and currently is always trying to automate systems or tasks for efficiency and cost cutting.

Microsoft Office eliminated the need for bookkeepers, clerks, and secretaries.  The personal computer eliminated the need for typists.  Machines allowed one farmer to do the work of twenty or thirty laborers who did all the weeding, plowing, seeding, and cultivating of crops.

But every time an industry for general laborers was destroyed, the economic boon from increased productivity and better valued services have grown other sectors and thus increased the amount of jobs and better quality jobs available to the population.  Jobs are not a fixed pie and have never followed the fixed pie fallacy/model.

You don't need to work in a coal mine or factory in order to make a living anymore.  More people have access to higher education and more specialized disciplines that offer much better working conditions than previous generations.  With automation, goods and services are MUCH cheaper than they were to previous generations.  Do you think we didn't erase tens (if not hundreds) of thousands of jobs during the process of giving you access to the entire world's library of music, movies, books, etc with an internet connection, few taps of your finger on your smartphone, and $30 a month?

So, unless you're claiming that NOW is this actual time where automation will wipe out all human capital, then recognize that this is just the same song and dance has has repeated itself since the steam engine was invented.

For these jobs that require low, or even no skilled labor the robot will 100% win in the long run.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@AndrewTSq You’re comparing two completely different things here.

​A fixed conveyor sorter doing 20k/hr only works on a rigid track in a purpose-built facility. You can’t use a conveyor belt to unload irregular freight off a truck, navigate cramped legacy shelving, or adapt on the fly.

​Humanoids and AMRs aren't meant to beat a stationary cross-belt machine at raw linear speed—they're built for flexible 24/7 edge labor where fixed automation physically can't go. Plus, modern humanoids (Unitree, Tiangong, etc.) already handle pick-and-place cycles in under 2 seconds with 360°/s joint speeds, zero downtime, and no shift breaks.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@AndrewTSq Fair point on early Unitree dev kits—the early joints definitely weren't built for 24/7 industrial duty cycles yet. Wheeled AMRs with cobot arms are great on flat ground, but once you need to reach top shelves or deep into trailers, the center of gravity forces the base to be too wide for tight aisles. I'm convinced not many of you never work at package facilities or know what they're like on the inside. There's never endless amounts of packages. Trailers will arrive on time, early or even late. 

People will always unload the trailers, because the packages are mixed, and in shambles. The conveyor belt can speed up or slow down, it won't matter. The robot is mainly touching bag packages, which you just have to flip over. As for boxes, the package tag can be on either 4 corners. 

Not saying robots can be efficient and help workers, but machines already have that figured out by sorting down conveyer belts. And even then machines make mistakes... And who has to fix machine mistakes? 

I don't know what company needs a robot to simply flip a package anyway. Usually there's a scanner that will sort through all four angles. If you need a million dollar robot to do that, then I think it's time to hang it up lol.

Ultimately, from what I could find online, the robot costs around $200,000, while a human worker costs about $20 an hour. However, the robot doesn't need a break, won't need a vacation, doesn't need to stop, and can work 24 hours a day. That is replacing a wage of roughly $22.83 an hour. The benefits of it running 24 hours a day and its cost versus the human worker make it a no-brainer, even if it is less efficient.

snippet.textDisplay:
​The final score: The human barely won, sorting 12,924 packages compared to the robot's 12,732 (a difference of just 192 packages).

​The physical toll: After 10 continuous hours at an extreme pace, the worker ended the test with blistered fingers and severe forearm pain from the unnatural physical strain.

​The company's reaction: Right after the challenge, the CEO posted on social media: "This is the last time a human wins," highlighting that the machine doesn't get tired or need breaks.

​Reflecting on the situation:

​Reducing humans to components: Forcing an operator through a 10-hour marathon just to see if they can beat a machine by a fraction of a second reduces human labor purely to "performance metrics."

​Distorting technology's purpose: Automation should exist to eliminate backbreaking, repetitive labor—preventing workers from destroying their hands over a 10-hour shift—not to turn the workplace into an arena where humans must push past physical limits just to justify their existence or paycheck.

​Value beyond the stopwatch: Human work cannot be measured in saved fractions of a second. Reducing everything to raw execution speed completely wipes out dignity, health, quality of working life, and the social role of human employment.

The scary thing about this is how a business owner especially someone running a large company is going to look at it. They’re constantly trying to maximize productivity, which ultimately means maximizing profits. Even if the human is faster right now, the owner is thinking long term. I don’t have to pay the robot an hourly wage. It doesn’t call out sick, take vacation, need breaks, require workers’ comp, health insurance, or other employee benefits. It can potentially work around the clock without many of the costs and complications that come with human labor. 

That’s the crazy part. It’s not necessarily about whether the robot can outperform a human today it’s about whether it becomes cheaper, more reliable, and more profitable over time. And once it does, that could completely change the workforce.

My company sends about 100 pieces of mail per week. Almost all are checks to pay our vendors. About 4 years ago, we started getting a few each month returned to sender for incorrect address, but the addresses were fine. Worse, some mail disappeared.  It costs us to cancel checks and reissue, and our work can be delayed if a vendor withholds service.  I went to our post office to ask why this was suddenly a huge problem.  The postal worker told me that their new automation will read an incorrect address but pick up a different envelope.
This started under Louis DeJoy, a tRump appointment.  tRump has had a lot to say about fully privatizing the USPS, and the appointment was made while tRump raged against mail-in ballots.

I have a degree in Electronics Technology majoring in Industrial automation. I was a member of Robotics International. If you think this video is a win you're wrong. That human will need breaks, lunch, days off, heat, cooling, medical insurance, retirement, safety considerations, and more. The robot needs none of that, and does almost the same amount of work. The arguement isn't about production. It's about economics. 
You better find a new way to fight this. Robots powered with AI will out pace humans very quickly. Doing so will destroy the consumer base companies need to sell their products. But each is looking for profit, social considerations come in dead last. Until it starts to impact their bottom line they will continue to push workers out for more profit. If they don't the CEO will be replaced until they do.
 It won't be until we hit a tipping point that they will even admit they're creating a problem. By then it will likely be too late. The economy will crash without consumers. But they need jobs to be consumers.

A difference of just 192 packages is not merely a narrow margin; it's a significant lead, especially considering that he wasn't even exerting maximum effort compared to the robot, which was consistently assisted remotely by multiple humans throughout the entire process.

Some might argue that a robot can operate around the clock without breaks, unlike a single human worker who requires 30 to 60-minute rest periods, time to commute home and rest afterward, as well as various leaves such as sick leave, vacation days, FMLA, and paternity leave.

However, they often overlook the critical issue of robot downtime due to breakdowns, viruses, or malfunctions—inevitabilities in automated systems. When such failures occur, who is responsible for diagnosing the problem, reprogramming, repairing, or replacing the robot without halting the entire assembly line or workload? The answer is humans.

snippet.textDisplay:
Here's the problem people do not see...

Sure... Humans beat Robots in a timed session...

But...

Humans require breaks, sleep, pto, sick-leave, benefits, etc.

Robots require scheduled maintenance, a power bill, and small team of techs, and can run all day.


That 194 package difference for 1 human shift goes out the window the moment the human clocks out... the robot can stay working withhout changing pace, needing a break for food, restroom, smoke, etc... doesn't have a complaint to lodge, etc. 

I would assume they have at least a 100,000hr lifespan on average. Over that 100,000hrs, the company saves ~$2.79 BILLION, and productivity goes up, cost of operation goes down, corporate profits soar, and shareholders are happy... but now there's 1 less worker being paid, 1 less wage being earned. 

Sure... we can put robots in these types of jobs... because it actually makes sense. The amount of time training is fractional, the cost is fractional, and the profit is exponential. I would assume the error rate is within 1-2% of human error rate these days... which isn't bad.

So... W for Robots in areas that require no critical thinking.

snippet.textDisplay: Assuming a person makes $17 an hour the company pays closer to $50 an hour in labor costs including matching tax contributions, pay, insurance on the employee, and cost of training. So a $500,000 robot will cost significantly less Than a human employee over the average operational lifespan of that unit. That doesn't even touch on cost savings from reduced down time due to absenteeism, support staff like HR, lawsuits for personal injury or sexual harassment. There is zero downside to fully automating as many positions as possible even at the expense of productivity due to profit retention from having fewer living people.

This all reminds me of the old fable of Paul Bunyon.  The mythically large giant of a man who could cut down a tree faster than any other man alive.  

One day an inventor wanted to prove the worth of his rail laying piston steam machine by pitting it up against Paul in a contest to see who can lay down track faster.

And continues to win in all things mechanic vs hand.  But the science does have to exist.

snippet.textDisplay:
Winning by 192 packages is NOT "barely winning" - here's why:
Say this guy works 1 of these full work shifts per day. 
He gets 192 more packages done. 
In 10 work days that is 1,920 packages difference. 
In 365 work days that is 70,080 packages difference. 
And he's doing this CASUALLY. Not even trying. 
If your company is sending out 70,000 FEWER packages PER PERSON and you have, let's say, a staff of 100 people in this factory, you are looking at SEVEN MILLION FEWER PACKAGES A YEAR with the robot. 

Now, you might think "but the robot can work 24/7"  - except...not really. Parts wear out with repeated movements, sensors go bad, and someone has to be around to make sure there's no massive errors going on with this thing or there's a lot of very upset customers out there, which means it still has to be supervised constantly, which means it's still only going to be operating during work hours. How often those parts must be changed out, how much the parts cost, the cost of electricity to run it, etc., these are all factors as well. MISTAKES per 1,000 units also matters. 

So, no, that's not "barely winning" when you extrapolate to the number of staff in a larger facility over longer spans of time. It actually begins to become a HUGE difference to the point it can break your business. 

With more ADVANCED robotics that will change, but with THIS one, not so much.

snippet.textDisplay: @vshah1010 That's a valid concern about transition friction, but it doesn't refute the underlying claim - historically, every major automation wave (agriculture, manufacturing, computerization) prompted the same "this time the skills gap is too large" objection, yet labor markets adapted, partly through new job categories requiring different, often lower, skill thresholds than the technology itself (maintenance, oversight, data labeling, logistics coordination), not just competing directly with degree-holders on the technical work. The claim isn't that displaced workers become AI engineers overnight; it's that aggregate demand for labor shifts to new roles created by the technology's diffusion, a pattern borne out by long-run employment data despite each transition's genuine short-term hardship.

snippet.textDisplay:
Robots are still more cost effective in the long run. They don't call in sick, they reduce labor related costs such as social security contributions and taxes, and they can simply be taken offline when there aren't enough orders coming in. You can't do that with human workers, you can't just lay them off overnight, and you still have to keep paying their salaries according to the law or their contracts.

They also create fewer workplace-related issues. There are no unions to negotiate with, no demands for pay raises, and no employee disputes to manage.

Those are just a few points that came to mind immediately. If I took more time to think about it, I'd probably come up with many more reasons why robots can be a more practical and economical choice than human workers in many industries.

​​@iiSaYeDxAy trabajos que nunca podrán hacer los robots.

Las cariñosas sobrevivieron a la edad media, la edad de piedra, la revolución industrial, el boom tecnológico... Pero una robotzuela podría reemplazarlas en cualquier momento.

Si me dieras más tiempo podría hacer una lista más completa sin dudas sería larga.

snippet.textDisplay:
It’s not about how fast you work it’s about how long you can keep going. Sure, humans have bursts of energy, but as a worker yourself, imagine doing this 24/7, every single day of the week, praying you don’t get sick. It’s not ideal. That’s why most humans end up suffering and complaining. But companies don’t like complainers.

And here’s the funny, harsh truth: as a customer, I want my things ready I don’t care about you. Sounds brutal, but that’s the majority of customers. People like to think they’re noble, but they only hide it. If someone says it out loud, everyone attacks them but that’s the real reality.

We have 8 billion people in this world. Do you really think any one of them is thinking about your well-being as a worker? No. They’re thinking about how fast and efficiently they can get their stuff. If you get sick, no one cares. If you die, no one cares. You’ll make the news, then be forgotten. That’s the reality of working for a mega-corporation.

Honestly, I don’t even know why anyone would want to work like this. It’s hidden slavery, and you don’t even realize it. Let the robots do the job. Besides, companies don’t owe you work that’s why they can drop or lay you off without a second thought. That’s just how it is.

The fact is, when something more efficient than a human comes along, they’ll take it. That’s the goal. If a robot costs less and can work 24/7, nonstop, never gets sick, never needs a break it’s more efficient. It’s better.

So sure, go ahead and calculate how fast a human works you’re trying to make us look better than machines. But the funny thing is, it’s not about speed. It’s about endurance. And machines win at that, every time. So yeah it’s inevitable.  
Don’t try to use shields like it’s too expensive to maintain. It’s too expensive to build.  It’s not smart enough it’s there. These are all just delusions denial defences because those gaps are closing pretty fast technology doesn’t slow. Computer is back then was millions of dollars now computers just thousands of dollars. This is technology. What you’re supposed to be doing is not. Trying to go into the old system and look for work you should be making your own system taking advantage of the new system that’s currently being built and stop being a passive victim

snippet.textDisplay:
you should see the insanity of unloading a truck at home depot. I swear it looks like someone just packed floor the ceiling from the front to the back with zero regards for anything other than using all the space. 

I got asked to help out on unloading the truck a few times and the process was insane. Your basically tossing stuff on a roller if its small enough, using a machine for particularly big stuff and otherwise having someone carry the mid size stuff off by hand. The guy at the front of this is climbing on top of stuff to get things near the ceiling here and there and trying not to have the wall of product fall on him. Everyone outside by the roller is sorting the stuff onto carts by department number. 

All that to save a truck, but you have to wonder how many people are involved loading it like that because its a bunch of people for 90-120 minutes at the store. Then I go back to my usual stuff and the freight guys spend the night unloading those carts all over the store. Its nuts. It would take more trucks if they did it with sorted pallets, or sorted carts, but the manpower needed for the current method is terrible. 

Oh and the pace on that is much higher tempo than this.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@scott8908I have actually done this exact job at a unionized facility with empowered workers. The normal consistent pace you do for a complete shift is 1 package every 0.75-1.5 seconds. If you are going "1, 2, 1, 2" locking in on a package and then doing something with it second by second, you are already so slow that if you don't figure it out after a few days doing it and get used to it they will move you to a different position.

It is hard for people who haven't had jobs like this to imagine but it is 100% more difficult than any office job. Being at an office job is like being on vacation compared to a job like this.

I go into my job, mostly now I load package cars. I have 3 trucks with 8 shelves each that must be sequenced in order so the driver  an find and deliver packages efficiently. Packages are ranging form envelopes to 150+ LB couches in a box. I load about 200 packages per hour, and am slow for this. I pick up and put down about 15000 lbs on average in 3.5 hours.

There are people who start this job and it is so hard with regularity a certain number of people who start just walk out their first shift and don't come back. You cannot do anything but work at a fast pace the entire time you are working or else before you blink there will be an avalanche of packages and then you're fucked.

This work is the backbone of the economy. The entire economy does not happen without it. And it is incredibly difficult. And at least at unionized facilities like mine, for what we do for this country and for everyday people, we get free health insurance and a pension.

Theft is no longer an issue because your property can be replicated at no cost to you. You could create new galaxies just for you to explore, Conquer, fornicate or whatever you desire; (Gods).

Only then will freedom exsist for there will be no limitations.

snippet.textDisplay:
@Shaktimaaaaaan As an engineer, there’s this thing called unsupervised learning in the field of machine learning that definitively proves: yes, in theory and practice machine learning models can learn on their own without RLHF etc. But the reality is, the robot wasn’t working by itself on the livestream. They don’t use unsupervised learning for this sort of thing and that means almost constantly there is a human in the loop during training or even to reinforce or correct during operation. Figure wouldn’t risk a massive screw up on livestream running this 100% locally on the robot (if they even had models and silicon efficient enough); 90% chance or more they had tele-operation to intervene when things went wrong or to just do most of it outright. They are acting like it’s untethered but never show the bottom half of the robot. Given what I know about the silicon they can put in the robot, and the state of the art of model architectures/modalities they can use, I just don’t think it’s possible today for Figure as an organization and I sure as hell don’t think they’re ahead of Tesla in building a world model (or custom silicon hshahaha). It’s a really convincing stream for people who aren’t engineers but for those in the know, we see through it and realize it’s the CEO trying to generate hype. That’s cool and all, and prepares society for what I see is inevitable exponential progress, but the reality is the models themselves are massively behind the curve of hardware progress and AI is not close to proper recursive self improvement yet.

Generally what the other person said is right, though. Almost all these models use human teleoperation for rapid improvement and development; I highly doubt you can prove this wrong because it’s impossible. We don’t rlly use unsupervised learning anymore for this sort of thing. The big breakthrough that took ChatGPT from v2 to v3&4 was reinforcement learning with human feedback. Even IF this is all running locally on the robot (it isn’t), it wouldn’t be able to do that task (@80% efficiency either) without massive amounts of carefully curated human data. They hire tons of people to come into figure’s office to clean and sort shit for this reason.

@Shaktimaaaaaan I get defensive of AI hate too (I also get a lot of not reading allat responses, as you can tell haha). My career depends on AI success; hell, before ChatGPT came out I decided to study computer engineering precisely because of the prospect of artificial intelligence and what it would mean I get to contribute to in my career. For technology nerds AI has been the endgame prospective technology for a long time. 

Alpha fold is the real deal. Alpha fold was the biggest and first scientific breakthroughs to show the world how big a difference/impact this technology can make. Google has made it free to access for researchers and it’s solving problems for them daily. 

At the same time, Alpha fold is an example of precisely why the people building this stuff (Demis Hassabis) think it can be so dangerous though; any system significantly better than alpha fold at chemistry/biology in general could also theoretically wipe out humanity, and easily at that. At the same time, that same system could cure every form of cancer in an hour. Google the paperclip problem, for an example of it going wrong. 

The alignment problem- or making sure AI’s interests are aligned with Humans- is what decides whether this system acts out the good or bad scenario. I think these systems will be very very beneficial, but it’s not guaranteed. Companies racing to commercialize this stuff (like figure, here) risk getting alignment wrong for monetary benefit. 

Steve Jobs once said “computers are like bicycles for the mind.” I kind of take the same approach to AI; I don’t think it really can or should replace human brains and consciousness in many tasks. But it really is a technology that can ultimately either lead to utopia or hell for humanity. The problem is, do you want a company trying to make the most money making these decisions? When they make fake demos and then push out a product or service at the last moment with little preparation, they are taking a big risk with the alignment or safety of that ai tool/thing. I just tend to dislike companies that are trying to create hype by making things sound dangerous, or that take their demos to do the same thing. This is why.. I wasn’t attacking figure just bc it’s an ai company; I was attacking them because I’m worried about what this sort of behavior could lead to 

I only hope that whoever achieves AGI/ASI, has the best interests of Humanity at heart, not just the lining of their pockets.

And then there's the guys who "learn to survive" by intentionally trying to get a higher number with the least amount of physical work, which then leaves others to do more physical work, which the teamleader doesn't take into account and just considers you a slow worker. It's a shitfest, glad I stopped working there.

"Robots don't eat or sleep"
See, the thing is they do. Machines will need downtime for updates, maintenance, downtime, and charging if they're wireless. It's definitely not human levels of need, but to say they won't ever stop is ridiculous.

And now instead of paying for a worker, you're paying for the product, the software subscription, the power cost increase, the onsite engineer/IT guy.

If you make any one change to a system or have the tiniest error, there won't be a quick fix. And if one thing messes up in the change early on, it's going to mess everything up further along the line. You might even have to completely retrofit the entire system.

Not enough people play factory games to realize how often updates to products require entire factory retrofits.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@idk34388 Robots do cost a lot in some cases right now, but that’s because the technology is still new. Give it time, and it’ll become cheaper.just like every other technology when it first hits the market. So that argument doesn’t really hold up unless you can predict exactly how the future market will play out

Also, the robot shown in the video is human shaped, which isn’t very efficient in this scenario. It’ll likely be replaced by a specialized version designed specifically for the job, one that can do the work faster and more effectively

As for the point about many humans being qualified for this work...sure, just about anyone can do it. But who’s going to work 24/7 without food, sleep, or pay? Find me one person who would actually do that

The real advantage is that robots will be cheaper in the long run. You don’t have to pay them monthly, provide health insurance, or deal with all the other baggage that comes with human employees

A human might get sick or have a personal issue and not show up for a day, a week, or even longer. With a robot, you can replace it quickly.. . especially if the company keeps a backup on hand. It’s just a matter of swapping it out or replacing a single part

Humans also need rest and comfortable working conditions.. lots of AC, for example. Robots don’t need food and can operate in harsher environments if they’re designed for it.

Believe me, billionaires are pushing AI for a lot of reasons, and this is one of them. They’d love a worker who’s essentially a slave, but they’re held back by human limitations and human rights. So instead, they build robots that can do the job
