snippet.textDisplay:
​@2elpk depends on how the bean counters do their cost benefit analysis. If one robot replaces three individuals working for $17/hr then they save roughly $105k annually at the low end in wages alone not including overtime, plus insurance costs and any amenities they provide at no cost to those employees. A quarter million dollar robot would pay for its own capital cost in 2 or 3 years.

Operational costs are a little harder to estimate though, if the robot is inaccurate, unreliable, or the cost of servicing it is greater than anticipated it could very well be a money pit. The manufacturer might also try scamming the buyer with inflated costs by overcharging for software licensing or requiring maintenance be done by traveling technicians who are generally very expensive.

I suspect these gimmicky humanoid robots will fall into that category of overpriced and unproductive shiny bullshit that accomplish nothing but putting regular people out of work. More old-school robots tend to perform very well because they're purpose built and aren't intended to be used for any other function. The flaw with humanoid robots is that they struggle to accomplish tasks with the same efficiency as a real human (seen in the video). A machine designed for the express purpose of doing that job will outperform a general purpose humanoid bot every time, as will an actual human.

​@AprilPessy  you need to be educated on taxes and were they are collected from. Here's a little breakdown for you. 

Individual Income Taxes: ~40% to 53% of all collections, making it the largest source of U.S. revenue.

Payroll Taxes (Social Insurance): ~24% to 33%, funding Social Security and Medicare.

Consumption Taxes: ~17%, primarily driven by state and local general sales taxes and federal excise taxes (like gas and alcohol).

Property Taxes: ~11%, largely collected by local governments to fund schools and municipal services.

Corporate Income Taxes: ~8%, levied on corporate profits.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@colonelradec5956The main problem is going to be the cost.... Let me give you a small example of the high cost. Not even including dynamic movement or muscular tension. The human arm has 7 principal degrees of freedom. AKA seven different pivot points. That means just for one arm would be seven servos. That's not including the wrist and the fingers and the hand; adding those brings it up to 27 principal degrees of freedom. The human body contains over 240 distinct mechanical degrees of freedom in total, including all limbs, neck and spine. Robotic systems usually simplify this to roughly 80 to 90 primary degrees of freedom. A high-torque, small, low-weight servo is gonna cost an average of $500, so just in raw material of servos, a humanoid robot would start at $45,000. That's also 80 to 90 different failure points..... So at the point we are at, it's not a technological road block, its infrastructure cost and materials..... So, doing some rough math based on other advanced humanoid robots, we are looking at about $50,000 to $100,000 in initial startup cost, an additional $15,000 per year in maintenance moving parts, and about $1,500 a year on power. The physical and operational lifespan of a humanoid robot ranges between 5 and 8 years under active, daily workplace conditions (not 24/7 operation because that would double the power draw and double the maintenance). So over the course of 8 years, this robot will cost you $142K..... With that math, the robot is working on a minimum wage. $13 an hour. Meaning the only places that you will see these things used will most likely be warehouses and factories. Even then, they won't be that common because, as I said, purpose-built robots are cheaper and more efficient. Even though $13 an hour to operate is extremely low, affordable factory lines have robots that operate at less than $8 an hour and foreign labor can come in as low as $2 an hour. The cost is far too much for anybody to actually use inside their home. Certain electronics that are based on principles and don't really change much will also not be affected by inflation. The TV is a great example, technology wise it has gone leaps and bounds. Practically, it's still the same system, which is smaller lights. Smaller parts, smaller power sources. So, in principle it's still the same, and because of that a TV costs the same in 1970 as it cost in 1990 as it cost in 2010 and as it cost in 2026....

​​@OldGlory4648I'ma address these points 1 by 1 so your not to scared 

1."Never needs a break" - these humoid robots have 90 degrees of freedom all 90 have high torque servos that touch and move meaning it needs regular downtime

2."Never complains" - robots have error codes, and robots are like women, they complain a lot, especially about running too hot or cold 

3."Never gets tired" - this is a bad thing because being tired is your body telling you to stop, this just increases risk of ruin.

4."Never slack on the Job" - Human error and robotic error are drastically different. Humans will be a little lazy, robots will stack boxes 0.2 degrees off for hours causing a catastrophic failure. 

5."Never spaces out" - what do you think happens during a power or network outage? 

6."Never gets Injured" - If we equate injury to maintenance. The average cost of healthcare for one human in a year is only 1/5 of the average cost of regular maintenance on injured bots. 

7."Never takes sick days" some of these "injuries" require trained technicians and can take a single bot out  of service for possible days, equating to sick days. 

8."Never asks for a raise" - This is actually the part that companies are going to hate, Companies go years at a time before giving workers raises, that's why the average wage has barely gone up compared to inflation. These companies will have no say in the inflation of parts and new bots, at a yearly 2% inflation, these bots will quickly become more expensive than general labor.

10. "Never looks for better employment opportunities" - I mean yea but if these bots only have a lifespan of 5 to 8 years they are still cycling the workforce out at about the same rate of humans. 

There's a lot of things that can cook us. Humanoid robots are nothing more than a fantasy. They're just never going to be as practical as purpose-built robots or as cheap.

And because it is NOT a perfect technology and business is on the line, it cannot be left to run unsupervised lest something go wrong, it break down, etc. - which means it's NOT going to run 24/7 - it's going to run during work hours when it can be supervised. And, 192 packages difference in one shift is 70,080 difference PER WORKER per year. Over the course of a year comparing 100 employees in a factory to 100 robots, this would mean shipping over 7 MILLION fewer packages with the robots. 

"Cheaper"? Do you have any idea how much that thing COSTS to buy and maintain? One joint gets worn down and that thing is out of commission possibly for hours or days. It's not replacing people YET. ALSO, technically, there is nothing stopping a production facility from having people on the line 24/7. You just swap out a worker every 8 hour shift, 3 times a day. One guy gets the night shift, one guy gets morning, one guy gets daytime. 

Suppose the employee is making $10 an hour. There are jobs that pay that low in the US and even lower, and plenty of illegal immigrants to do them. 

That's a cost of $240 per day to pay those 3 employees across 3 shifts. $87,600 a year. 

But the ROBOT likely costs $500,000 per unit. 
It costs money to keep the power on. 
Let's say the joint wears out at the elbow after so many motions and it gets replaced....maybe every 1,000 hours or 41.6 days. that's ABOUT 9 times a year you're replacing something. Minimum, lots of moving parts in it, lots of ways it can break. But let's SAY it's only 9. 

If each replacement takes that unit off-line for 24 hours, that's 3 working shifts, that's close to 30,000 packages that don't go through. You could swap in another unit, but that means you ALSO need another $500,000 unit on STANDBY which is another expense. 

Suppose there are 100 human workers vs 100 robots. 
For the 100 robots, you'd need a NUMBER of standby units, likely each also priced at the same $500,000 (what, did you really think you were getting this thing for CHEAP?) - ideally, 1 standby per unit. That's MILLIONS of dollars more. JUST IN CASE any one of them breaks down, you NEED a standby or you lose precious processing time and thousands of packages do not get shipped which can be very costly if you have to issue refunds or orders get cancelled. 

100 human workers PER full work shift (8 hours)  would put out 7 million more packages a year than the robots at this rate. Or, 21 million if there are 3 shifts and people getting swapped in every 8 hours, at a cost of $87,600 a year assuming a pay rate of $10 an hour. 

That is CONSIDERABLY more work done AND cheaper than it would be to BUY the 100 advanced robots AND stand-by units AND repair parts for any breakdowns AND pay the power bill to run them all. And are they plugged into a wall? if not, their battery isn't going to last very long which means they'll need long recharge periods, which again means you need fully charged standby units which ALSO cost a lot of money. 

Let me put it this way: if each robot costs $500,000, and you need 100 of them plus, let's say, 100 standby units, one for each in case of needing to take one down for repairs here and there, that is $500,000 * 100 * 2 = 
$100 MILLION DOLLARS for the 100 robots plus 100 standby units. 

THEN you have to account for repair /parts costs. Let's say 9 repairs per unit per year, maybe costing $5000 per repair, that's $45,000 per unit per year or for the 100 active units, $4.5 MILLION in repairs per year. 

We'll even ignore the power bill. 

SO all told you are looking at an INITIAL cost of $100 million dollars for all the robots plus their backups, PLUS $4.5 million in repairs, 

COMPARE that to the $87,600 for paying 3 illegal immigrants $10 an hour, each getting an 8 hour shift for a total of $240 a day in costs, or $87,600 a year per work station. 

Over 100 WORK stations, to replace the 100 robots, that is $8.76 MILLION for the HUMAN employee cost vs $104.5 million for the robots.

EVEN IF you assumed each robot only cost 1/5th that, say, $100,000 a unit (not happening), the total cost would still be over $20 million for the robots. 

Even IF you assumed they each only cost $100,000 and you don't allow for ANY stand-by units so you ONLY buy 100, that's still about $10 million in costs not including the $4.5 million in repairs. Vs the $8.76 million for the humans. So even under the OPTIMAL scenario for the robots you're still looking at it costing for year 1 almost TWICE as much as the humans running 3 8 hours shifts a day at $10 an hour. 

But again you KNOW those robots are not only going to cost $100,000 and you KNOW they need standby units for when repairs are needed or breakdowns happen -  so the initial cost for the robots is still more likely to be closer to the $100 million figure not including the power bill and repair costs. 

In order to pay for itself over humans being paid $10 an hour working 8 hour shifts 3x a day (3 different workers getting swapped out every 8 hours), at an initial up front cost of $100 million, and accounting for the $4.5 million in repairs over 100 units per  year, the remaining (over 90 million dollars) difference would take the robots working day in, day out for ....

well let's do the mathematics:

$8.76 million for the 100 human stations per year. 
4.5 million in repair costs for the 100 robots per year. 
A difference of $4.17 million.

So NOT including the $100 million up front cost of all the robots AND their stand-by replacement units, the robots would be $4.17 million cheaper (not including power bills of course) than the 100 human stations running 24/7 to maintain. 

Knowing THIS, how long does it take to make up for the $100 million up front cost of all the robot units?

100 / 4.17 million per year = 23.98 YEARS for the robots to ACTUALLY pay off that $100 million up front cost difference with their savings over humans. 

Even if you assume HALF the cost per robot unit or that there are very foolishly NO stand-by units purchased , that's STILL a $50 million up front cost plus $4.5 million a year in repairs at the above rates, which will STILL take almost 12 years to start having an advantage over the humans. 

Now, you may try to argue $10 is too low an hourly wage, but clearly you're not familiar in that case with the minimum wage in many parts of the U.S., much less the world. Nationally, the minimum wage is well below $10 an hour. And again, there's always a migrant worker willing to take that job even if locals don't. And again, even if you presumed the robots can work 24/7, so can the humans if you just have 3x 8 hour shifts, a different worker coming in each 8 hours, each of them making $10 an hour for 8 hours. 

But there's one MORE thing you should know:
that's not a fully automated robot. It's remotely operated by a human being. SO. It was never a real thing to begin with. 

So unless those things are operating over a quarter of a century, at the above costs, they're not beating 3 employee shifts a day at $10 an hour. In FACT, it'd still take them over a decade at that rate to beat a $20/hour employee rate. And sooner or later, each unit will break down and have to be replaced a lot sooner than 24 years, which means ANOTHER very expensive up front purchase. 

And, this is all without factoring in the power bill to run 100 of them vs the snickers bars to run some humans.

22k moron liked this! LMFAO @ human ignorance!

The claim that robots are simply 'cheaper than humans' ignores the entire infrastructure required to keep them operating.

Robots don't install themselves, program themselves, repair themselves, calibrate themselves, or redesign themselves when production changes.

Every automated sorting system requires:

• Software developers to write and update the control software.
• Automation engineers to integrate new equipment.
• PLC programmers to troubleshoot and modify logic.
• Electrical and mechanical technicians to repair breakdowns.
• Spare parts inventories, replacement motors, sensors, cameras, belts, actuators, and controllers.
• IT staff to maintain networks, servers, cybersecurity, and databases.
• Human supervisors to monitor performance, quality, and safety.
• Operators to clear jams, reload materials, inspect errors, and intervene when automation fails.

Robots also require electricity 24/7, scheduled maintenance, software licensing, insurance, downtime during failures, and eventual replacement when they become obsolete.

A human employee can adapt to a new task in minutes. Reprogramming an automated system can take engineers days or weeks and cost thousands of dollars.

Automation doesn't eliminate people. It replaces some low-skill jobs with fewer, higher-paid technical jobs while adding significant capital, maintenance, and engineering costs.

Working 24/7 doesn't mean producing 24/7. Machines require preventive maintenance, calibration, cleaning, inspections, repairs, software updates, and experience unexpected failures. When one critical robot fails, an entire production line can stop. Humans don't usually cause an entire warehouse to grind to a halt because one person called in sick.

I was running CNC robots 20 years ago. The cost to this day is still exceeding what costs would have been maintaining human operators. 

Every 12 hours shift a robot was down literally cost the company north of $25k a day!

Not only did the human win.

But the human does not require a team to keep it operating!

The human doesn't require a programmer, a maintenance crew, expensive parts, or another capable and man-made/maintained human to keep them going.

The human by far is cheaper unless scaled to a specific point, and then still they are running from a negative for a foreseeable future.

Just from the surface alone.

The robot still requires a human to operate it.
The robot still require parts to stay running. Which require humans to manufacture from design.
The robot still requires humans to maintain it.

I think some of you have no idea how robots work or how much they cost to create and maintain.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@EliteShorter This is actually one of Karl Marx's ideas for Higher Stage Communism. The idea starts when technology would drive necessary labor time down to a minimum where human labor is increasingly excluded from direct production, leaving humans as regulators and watchmen. He theorized that this displacement could create the conditions for a post work, post scarcity society if the tools belonged to society as a whole. Marx argued that under capitalism, technology is not neutral. It's shaped by power relations and used to extract surplus value. Marx then argued that once technology matures enough to eliminate scarcity, society can move past wages, prices, and money entirely as there's no more need. "In communist society, where nobody has one exclusive sphere of activity but each can become accomplished in any branch he wishes, society regulates the general production and thus makes it possible for me to do one thing today and another tomorrow, to hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening, criticize after dinner, just as I have a mind, without ever becoming hunter, fisherman, herdsman or critic." So essentially, after automation becomes efficient enough to have an overabundance of things, Humans wouldn't work, there wouldn't be social classes as the automation doesn't belong to 1 single person or group of people but everyone, and you get what you need from a community "pot". "From each according to their ability, to each according to their needs." Now I'm not agreeing with this, and I never seen America ever ending up like this but it's quite an interesting concept to think about especially with how fast AI is evolving. I mean, would it really be so bad in that type of society where you can simply live how we were intended to do and not work just for a paycheck to survive? Another thing to remember is that Karl Marx didn't see Capitalism as a pure enemy but a necessary evil, a stepping stone as Capitalism leads to Socialism which leads to Communism.

@littleluo23510 Alright, at first it sounds like a funny idea. But real talk: if I had a gadget like that, the bare minimum requirement would be that the built-in video camera can be accessed live via my phone at any time. And since I don't really trust these devices to have any actual practical use, the minimum function would be roaming around the rooms so I can check at any time while I'm away if anything unusual has happened.

And that is precisely what would cause massive problems here in Germany. Neither monitoring people in nursing care nor recording kids in their room when you're actually in the house is legally straightforward under data protection laws. Even small children have privacy rights. When it comes to monitoring a patient in need of care who might not even have the capacity to consent anymore, you'd need explicit written authorization from a court-appointed legal guardian—not to mention if visitors or nursing staff were to be filmed. The legal regulations in Germany regarding this are borderline insane.

snippet.textDisplay:
Humans will never arrive. Musk is the modern day Barnum.

**Is Starship Going to Safely Deliver Humanity to Mars?**

Buckle up, folks. After marinating in the details, you’ll realize this whole endeavor isn’t just high-stakes — it’s a **high-stakes clown show** with rockets. 🤡🚀

1. **Radiation shielding?** Economically speaking, we’d need a 14-foot-thick wall of water wrapped around the ship like the galaxy’s most expensive pool noodle. Spoiler: Nobody’s paying for that. So… vibes-based shielding it is.

2. **Everyone’s getting cancer and kidney dialysis on the way.** Six months of cosmic rays turning your DNA into abstract art. Your kidneys will file for early retirement. 

3. In 50+ years of deep space talk, we’ve sent *zero* live mammals on a full Mars round trip. Not one brave mouse, hamster, or influencer’s emotional support chihuahua. That should tell you something.

4. But sure, let’s load up some optimistic, heavily screened humans and yeet them toward the Red Planet like it’s a particularly ambitious one-way Uber.

5. **Stay tuned** for the reality show: *Will They Make It to Mars Before Their Cells Mutiny?* (Brought to you by whoever’s still alive at touchdown.)

6–7. Deep space radiation laughs at our best efforts. Earth gets by with a magnetic field *and* a 25-mile-thick atmosphere blanket. Starship? It’s bringing optimism and some fancy carbon fiber. 

8. Reproduction in deep space? Forget it. We’re not building a colony — we’re building the galaxy’s most expensive singles cruise with no return policy.

9. At the end of the day, this might just be the most expensive publicity stunt in history so one very online CEO can become the world’s first trillionaire. *Step right up, folks!*

10. We were all raised on sci-fi and 1950s Disney propaganda (courtesy of some very complicated German engineering talent). The brainwashing is now generational. We clap for rockets like trained seals.

11. Jesus said you’ll know them by their fruits. Currently, the fruit looks suspiciously like a very expensive fireworks show with radiation sprinkles.

12–13. The spiritual predecessor to all this? A 1955 documentary literally titled *Conquest of Space*. The vibes were *chef’s kiss* Nazi-chic space opera.

14. Deep space hates life. It hates it in creative, inventive, and relentless ways. We know this. We just choose to ignore it while humming the *Interstellar* soundtrack.

15. Meanwhile, every Starship launch spews 1,300 tons of methane/oxygen exhaust straight into the ozone layer’s living room. We should just rename that part of the atmosphere the **Ignorosphere**.

16. Future headline: “Musk Colonizes Mars, Gives Everyone on Earth Melanoma as a Bonus.”

17. “Peacetime rocketry” is the most optimistic oxymoron since “military intelligence.”

18. Every launch is quietly winning a slow war against the environment. The trees aren’t clapping back.

20. Has Elon ever shown you the magic radiation shield that actually works for six months straight? No? That’s because it lives in the same place as cold fusion and my six-pack.

21–25. The whole thing is part space adventure, part military flex, part Manifest Destiny cosplay. The radiation problem is brutal, polyethylene helps but doesn’t solve it, and secondary radiation from thick shields is the universe’s way of saying “nice try.”

**Bottom line:** Mars isn’t impossible. But pretending the journey is basically a long Uber ride with snacks is *peak* hopium. 

We’re not going as a mature, radiation-hardened interplanetary species. We’re going as the same chaotic, optimistic, slightly delusional primates who put a Tesla in space and called it a day. 

Godspeed, you beautiful idiots. I’ll be here watching with popcorn and a Geiger counter. 🍿☢️

snippet.textDisplay:
Pura conversa, a inviabilidade para manter esses robôs funcionando e absurda!

Segue:

O robô humanoide Tesla Optimus possui uma autonomia estimada de cerca de 8 horas de funcionamento sob condições de tarefas leves. 

Essa duração varia diretamente conforme a intensidade do uso e o modelo específico:

Autonomia por Cenário de Uso

Tarefas Leves ou Repouso: Entre 8 e 10 horas realizando atividades de baixa intensidade.

Trabalho Contínuo/Pesado: Entre 3 e 6 horas se o robô precisar caminhar rápido, carregar peso ou realizar cálculos intensivos de IA de forma ininterrupta.

Especificações Técnicas da Bateria

Capacidade: Equipado com um pacote de bateria de 2,3 kWh a 3 kWh (utilizando a tecnologia de células 4680 da Tesla) integrada no torso.

Consumo de Energia: Varia de 100W em modo ocioso até 500W em caminhada ou tarefas dinâmicas.

Recarga: O robô possui suporte a carregamento autônomo. Ao detectar bateria fraca, ele navega sozinho até uma base de recarga (docking station), restaurando a energia em um período que varia de 10 minutos a 1 hora (dependendo da potência da estação utilizada).

Não existem ainda essas estações de recarga, sem falar a engenharia absurda para captar e armazenar energia para essa frota de robôs. Isso sem falar que os raios solares chegam muito fraco devido a distância entre Marte e o Sol.

snippet.textDisplay:
Seems like the narrator of this video is asking the wrong question.

You can witness the publicity driving robotics development in China and then ask "what are they developing in private?" 😂

You're still stuck in the mindset that government drives innovation, when what it really does is launder stolen money.

The Chinese companies are largely private, for profit companies with real commercial applications and real private customers, from hotels to nursing homes.  Of course the government is interested in them as well, but the driving innovation is for profitable endeavors.

Boston Dynamics teased us for decades with tiny increments of innovation because BD never had any customers.  They had R&D budgets from the government that were bloated and tethered to zero tangible goals.  Military applications wait for the contractors to tell the Pentagon what they can do and how much.  Private buyers tell the industry what they're willing to pay for.

There are no "RFP's" in the private sector.  There are just businesses and individuals that will either pay for something or won't.  And any industry that wants to offer a solution must work their asses off to build products that make economic sense.

snippet.textDisplay:
Honestly it's all relative...
Just how the internet and car and electricity were all positive for humanity. They also carry similar drawbacks and drags on society.

Robotics and AI is no different. It's simply that it's new in our era so we tend to fear it.

Quick example. Imagine when the car came out! A loud clunky noisy thing that spewed fumes everywhere.
People worried about coach job losses and street sweepers and even horses, how would someone with a horse be able to co exist with these loud and dirty machines...
But a few decades and they started putting on mufflers, and designed them for a different type of road and so forth, so along with it came new tyres, new road types, new mechanical engineering, new coach companies and so on...
So sure some jobs went and became redundant, but new ones were created simply because tech changed...

Is a robot ever going to be economically viable enough to get into roof crawl spaces and walls and replace traditional trades? Maybe? But I'm pretty sure the day that starts happening humans will change housing to ACCOMMODATE the technology as well.
Just like the highways and telephone poles and so on.

Look at the USA. We mostly never know what’s coming next. The F-117 was a complete surprise, as was the B-2, the USA is secretive, it’s a powerful thing to learn, and they learnt this with the Manhattan Project…no one in the world suspected that they were actually building a nuclear bomb, that’s how secret it was, and this made the dropping of it even more chilling.

So, yeah, I’d say it’s more about propaganda than anything else…let’s also not forget that China can’t do anything like this without chips from Taiwan.

snippet.textDisplay:
Every single transformative technology in human history follows this exact same double-edged blueprint:

​Fire: Can burn down a settlement or keep a community warm and cook food.

​Electricity: Can power a hospital or execute someone in an electric chair.

​Nuclear Fission: Can power an entire clean-energy grid or wipe a city off the map.

​The Kitchen Knife: Can prepare a family meal or be used as a weapon.

​The common denominator in every single scenario isn't the metal, the code, or the physics, it's human intent and governance.

​When fearmongrers focus entirely on the "evil robot" narrative, they create a false dichotomy where the only option is to freeze progress out of fear. But stifling the technology doesn't magically eliminate human malice; it just deprives us of the very shields, like safer space exploration, non-lethal emergency response, and risk-free hazardous labor, that could save countless lives.

​At the end of the day, hardware has no moral compass. The ethics live entirely with the person holding the blueprints or the controller.

91 He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.

14 Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name.

15 He shall call upon me, and I will answer him: I will be with him in trouble; I will deliver him, and honour him.

snippet.textDisplay:
@_infinitsm_ Sorry, but you might want to check your vocabulary.  ETHICS and LAWS are two completely different categories of regulation. 

ETHICS are rules that exist within a smaller society--like the medical field, teaching, or even a church.  Break the rules, you get kicked out of your club.  That is why people talk about genetic engineering being "unethical" at times, might get your doctor's license pulled for something like that.

LAWS are rules that exist within a state--a government over a territory.  You break the laws, you end up in prison, get fined, or are executed.  Laws are absolute.  Such is why a state is sovereign.  

What you want to do is pass LAWS, not create ethics.  But, good luck with that:  The laws of your nation-state do not apply in others, and the people of other nation-states will GLADLY make Skynet to destroy your country in the next war!

snippet.textDisplay:
@HardHardMaster I won't guarantee what robots will look like in the future. But if we look back, just 30 years ago, mobile phones were huge bricks with short battery life, and could do almost nothing but make calls. Now, look at your smartphone; its computing power surpasses that of a mainframe computer from 30 years ago.

Once, I entered an elevator in a skyscraper, and the small elevator car contained five LED displays of different sizes. Remember those old-fashioned CRT monitors? Those huge boxes? Can you imagine putting five CRT monitors in an elevator car? They would take up all the space and get incredibly hot!

Twenty years ago, when I first used the internet, the speed was so slow that even a few small pictures took forever to load. Now, wow! Download speeds can reach 100MB/s!

Just three years ago, most humanoid robots couldn't even walk steadily. Now, look at these amazing robots!

I won't guarantee what robots will look like in the future, but it will likely exceed our imagination.

최종 조사 보고서: 국가 기관의 조직적 사이버 테러,  살인 방조 행위
​수신: 대한민국 검찰청, 국가인권위원회 (NHRCK), 법무부 귀중.
​I. 범죄 패턴 분석 ("20일 주기의 법칙")
​본 조사는 대한민국 내부에서 외국인들을 표적으로 삼아 발생한, 국가 기관과 연계된 조직적이고 치밀한 불법 사찰 및 청부 살해 혐의를 문서화한 것입니다. 가해자들은 **"20일의 한계선"**이라 명명된 엄격한 작전 프로토콜을 사용했습니다. 피해자인 에드워드 그리고리안(러시아 국적)과 타티아나 아르데슈빌리(러시아 국적)는 동일한 단계의 감시, 협박을 받았으며, 이후 자연사로 위장된 독극물 살해를 당했습니다.
​에드워드 그리고리안: 2022년 6월 3일 갈등 고조 \rightarrow 2022년 6월 11일~21일 급격한 건강 악화 후 사망 (18일 주기).
​타티아나 아르데슈빌리: 2023년 6월 1일 1차 화학 독극물 투여 시도 \rightarrow 2023년 6월 21일 최종 독극물 중독으로 사망 (20일 주기).
​정확히 1년의 시차를 두고 동일한 날짜(6월 21일)에 사망자가 발생한 수학적 반복성은 이것이 단순한 자연사가 아니라, 가해자들의 치밀한 작전 일정에 의해 실행된 조직적 살인임을 증명합니다.
​II. 디지털 위장 및 사이버 테러 (원격 제어 악용)
​감시 네트워크는 피해자들의 개인 모바일 기기(에드워드의 삼성 노트 5 포함)에 은밀히 내장된 고도의 원격 모니터링 및 관리(RMM) 소프트웨어를 악용했습니다.
​악성 시스템 위장: 해당 스파이웨어는 모바일 운영체제 내부에서 공식 긴급 서비스 명칭(NIS / 111 긴급 프로토콜)으로 위장하여 백그라운드에서 구동되었습니다. 이로 인해 일반적인 보안 백신을 우회할 수 있었습니다.
​데이터 조작 및 증거 인멸 ("클리닝"): 원격 운영자들은 조사관의 기기에 직접 접속하여 대화 기록을 수정하고, 디지털 증거를 삭제했으며, 의도적인 하드웨어 과열을 유도했습니다. 또한 e-People 등 공식 신고서의 텍스트를 실시간으로 변조하여 진술의 신빙성을 떨어뜨리려 획책했습니다.
​III. 디지털 마스터 키를 이용한 물리적 무단 침입
​디지털 감시는 주거지에 대한 물리적 침입과 완벽히 동기화되었습니다. 집주인(한국인)은 임차인이 집을 비운 시간을 원격으로 파악한 뒤, 디지털 마스터 칩키를 이용해 주거지에 무단 침입했습니다. 피해자 유족의 음성 녹취록에 따르면, 집주인은 무단 침입하여 주거지의. 

식수와 음식물에 화학적 독극물(신경독성 살충제/콤바트 프로페셔널 등)을 투여했고, 이는 피해자들의 급격한 장기 부전과 사망을 유발했습니다.
​IV. 출입국 데이터베이스 위조 및 불법 강제 출국

​I. 범죄 패턴 분석 ("20일 주기의 법칙")
​본 조사는 대한민국 내부에서 외국인들을 표적으로 삼아 발생한, 국가 기관과 연계된 조직적이고 치밀한 불법 사찰 및 청부 살해 혐의를 문서화한 것입니다. 가해자들은 **"20일의 한계선"**이라 명명된 엄격한 작전 프로토콜을 사용했습니다. 피해자인 에드워드 그리고리안(러시아 국적)과 타티아나 아르데슈빌리(러시아 국적)는 동일한 단계의 감시, 협박을 받았으며, 이후 자연사로 위장된 독극물 살해를 당했습니다.
​에드워드 그리고리안: 2022년 6월 3일 갈등 고조 \rightarrow 2022년 6월 11일~21일 급격한 건강 악화 후 사망 (18일 주기).
​타티아나 아르데슈빌리: 2023년 6월 1일 1차 화학 독극물 투여 시도 \rightarrow 2023년 6월 21일 최종 독극물 중독으로 사망 (20일 주기).
​정확히 1년의 시차를 두고 동일한 날짜(6월 21일)에 사망자가 발생한 수학적 반복성은 이것이 단순한 자연사가 아니라, 가해자들의 치밀한 작전 일정에 의해 실행된 조직적 살인임을 증명합니다.
​II. 디지털 위장 및 사이버 테러 (원격 제어 악용)

​악성 시스템 위장: 해당 스파이웨어는 모바일 운영체제 내부에서 공식 긴급 서비스 명칭(NIS / 111 긴급 프로토콜)으로 위장하여 백그라운드에서 구동되었습니다. 이로 인해 일반적인 보안 백신을 우회할 수 있었습니다.
​데이터 조작 및 증거 인멸 ("클리닝"): 원격 운영자들은 조사관의 기기에 직접 접속하여 대화 기록을 수정하고, 디지털 증거를 삭제했으며, 의도적인 하드웨어 과열을 유도했습니다. 또한 e-People 등 공식 신고서의 텍스트를 실시간으로 변조하여 진술의 신빙성을 떨어뜨리려 획책했습니다.

​디지털 감시는 주거지에 대한 물리적 침입과 완벽히 동기화되었습니다. 집주인(한국인)은 임차인이 집을 비운 시간을 원격으로 파악한 뒤, 디지털 마스터 칩키를 이용해 주거지에 무단 침입했습니다. 피해자 유족의 음성 녹취록에 따르면, 집주인은 무단 침입하여 주거지의.

snippet.textDisplay:
The STARFISH is a low-profile, modular six-limbed robotic platform built around a compact, articulated central chassis. Each of its six universal limbs can independently function as a wheel, articulated leg, stabilizer, manipulator, grappling/climbing appendage, or support strut, allowing the robot to dynamically change its configuration for roads, rubble, steep terrain, confined spaces, or obstacles. The chassis itself can contract, extend, twist, and change its stance, while distributed sensors provide near-360° environmental awareness and allow the robot to operate regardless of which direction is considered its “front.”
The core houses the power system, onboard computing/AI, communications, cooling, and modular payload bay, with interchangeable mission packages for reconnaissance, logistics, EOD/hazardous environments, search-and-rescue, policing, or military support. Its primary design principles are redundancy, graceful degradation, low center of gravity, terrain adaptability, and modular repair: losing or disabling one limb should not necessarily immobilize the platform, and damaged modules can theoretically be replaced without rebuilding the entire robot.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@lukesball1 yea, that's a true advantage to a "copy and paste" memory, but at the same time, it makes them all very predictable in the same ways.  Besides that, what i meant mostly is that robots sorta lack the very basic ability to clear/clean their sensors, where for humans it's instinctual/biological... robots in the future will definitely adapt, but most likely only when any particular problem actually happens.

However, Humans have an advantage here, because i can tell you what happened and then you are thinking what would i normally do in this instance, and what should i do differently....and then on top of that, what you might actually do, could be completely random from what you predetermined you would do.

It's very hard for computers to do random things... the algorithm for random numbers isn't even close to being any sort of true random, it just sorta simulates it.  One of the best random number generators out there actually uses a video feed of a wall of hundreds of lava lamps, and then based on how many of the blobs of goo inside are up or down, it generates a random number.  This is used for security encryption because it's unreasonably hard to predict hundreds of lava lamps and the thermodynamics of how they all react, being on the same wall. 

Computers are predictable... predictable because they don't do random... and this is partly why ai doesn't really create anything new, it just rehashes things it already knows... stuff it knows from humans, or info it created from human data. This is also why ai totally botches things and has no idea how bad it did.

For now, humans still have the advantage of being random and creative, hopefully when it counts the most.

snippet.textDisplay:
@Mr.Ysk401 You talk about research, I wonder how much research you have done yourself on this topic, or you are just pretending very hard like you know what you are talking about on this subject for some reason? Just to humor you, I shared this video with ChatGPT and your last comment, below is a more detailed response from it, knock yourself out:

That comment is overstating the evidence. The reality is more nuanced:

Some humanoid robot demonstrations are fully autonomous.
Some are partially autonomous (e.g., autonomous balance and locomotion, but a human selects high-level commands).
Some are fully teleoperated (a human directly controls the robot's movements).

Just watching a video is not enough to determine which mode is being used.

Regarding the specific argument:

"They all move the same. They all require a human operator."

Moving similarly is not evidence of teleoperation. There are several other explanations:

Shared motion libraries
If every robot runs the same walking, punching, and recovery algorithms, they will naturally look similar.
Human athletes trained by the same coach also tend to have similar techniques.
Safety constraints
Humanoid robots are expensive (often tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars).
Developers deliberately restrict movements to stable, tested motions instead of letting reinforcement learning generate completely unpredictable attacks.
Competition rules
Many robot competitions require standardized hardware and software limits so that teams compete fairly on specific capabilities rather than brute-force experimentation. The URKL league itself states it is designed to evaluate motion control, balance, perception, and decision-making under standardized conditions.

"If AI was controlling it, it would use everything in the robot's body."

This isn't how modern robotics works.

An autonomous robot does not simply invent new martial arts techniques because AI is enabled.

Engineers define:

allowable joint angles
torque limits
balance constraints
collision avoidance
legal attack motions
safety rules

The AI chooses within those constraints.

This is similar to AlphaGo. AlphaGo doesn't suddenly move pieces off the board—it plays within the rules.

"They're punching the air, therefore no AI."

Missing punches actually proves very little.

Even state-of-the-art humanoids still have difficulty with:

estimating opponent motion
camera latency
depth perception
whole-body balance during impacts
recovering after being hit

These limitations exist whether the robot is autonomous or teleoperated.

Human beginners in boxing also miss punches frequently.

Humanoid Robots - Unitree G1 & H1
For their more advanced line of humanoid robots, AI is the core of their operational functions:

Onboard AI Computing: Their humanoid robots are equipped with high-powered processors (such as the NVIDIA Jetson Orin with up to 100 TOPS of computing power) so that AI and deep learning algorithms can run directly on the robot without the need for a constant internet connection (offline deployment).

In short, the AI ​​functions in Unitree robots are not just visual gimmicks; they also include autonomous motion control, intelligent navigation, and voice and gesture interaction to support research, education, and industry needs.

snippet.textDisplay:
@thehiddenyogi8557 You're analyzing without prior knowledge, here.

The joke is that Nokia phones are indestructible because they were known to be oddly resistant to damage, and had crazy long battery life. This led to people making videos where they strapped a Nokia phone to a handle and used it successfully as a hammer, along with many other clips of similar nature, that all play on the oddly high durability of the device. They aren't truly indestructible, but they are very long lasting and so is the joke around that fact.

The Twisted Tale of the Rubik's Cube

Where It All Began (1974)

The Rubik's Cube was unleashed upon an unsuspecting world in 1974 by a Hungarian architecture professor named Ernő Rubik.


His original goal was shockingly innocent: he wanted a 3D structural model to help explain spatial geometry to his architecture students. Little did he know, he wasn’t teaching geometry—he was crafting a psychological torture device.

It took Ernő himself an entire month to solve his own invention the first time. During that month, he likely stared blankly at a wall while questioning every life choice that led him to that exact coordinate in spacetime.

What Are They Actually Made Of?

While manufacturers claim they are made of standard ABS plastic, metal springs, and PVC stickers, anyone who has ever owned one knows the terrifying truth. 

Modern speedcubes are actually constructed from:

 Shattered Hope: The primary structural polymer, harvested directly from the souls of people who peel off the stickers to "solve" it.

 Lubricant of Despair: A mysterious industrial-grade silicone oil that somehow ends up all over your desk, your hands, and your life choices, despite you never having opened the core.

 Acoustic Torment: Specifically engineered internal plastic clicky-parts tuned to a frequency that instantly summons a migraine and annoys everyone within a 50-mile radius.

 Pure Spite: The microscopic tension springs inside that hold the center caps on are wound by malicious gnomes whose sole joy in life is watching a grown adult burst into tears because the orange edge piece went where the green corner piece was supposed to live.

The Aftermath


Today, billions of these colorful plastic cubes exist worldwide. They are responsible for millions of bruised thumbs, countless broken friendships, and an underground subculture of teenagers who can solve them in under four seconds while blindfolded, riding a unicycle, and eating a burrito—thus proving that humanity is evolving, just not the way you’d think.

o rigorously formalize the vehicle development lifecycle, we must transition from high-level abstractions to the granular thermodynamic, structural, and aeromechanical governing equations that dictate orbital launch vehicle synthesis.Phase 1: Mission Architecture, Trajectory Optimization, and Delta-V BudgetingThe synthesis of any launch vehicle begins with the definition of the mission profile and the subsequent evaluation of the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation:\(\Delta V=I_{sp}g_{0}\ln \left(\frac{m_{0}}{m_{f}}\right)\)Where m₀ is the initial wet mass, \(m_{f}\) is the dry structural mass plus payload, and \(I_{sp}\) is the effective net vacuum specific impulse. To establish a baseline architecture, you must execute a multi-disciplinary design optimization (MDO) loop:Gravity and Atmospheric Drag Losses: Compute the integrated loss budget over a simulated gravity turn trajectory. The true velocity increment required to achieve a specific Low Earth Orbit (LEO) insertion must account for non-conservative forces:\(\Delta V_{req}=V_{orbital}+\int \frac{D(t)}{m(t)}dt+\int g(r)\sin (\gamma (t))dt+\text{Steering\ Losses}\)Where D(t) is aerodynamic drag, γ(t) is the flight path angle, and g(r) is the local gravitational acceleration.Payload Boundary Conditions: Define the structural, thermal, and acoustic environment of the payload fairing. Specify the maximum allowable mechanical impedance, random vibration spectrum (PSD G²/Hz), and maximum quasi-static load factors (g-loads) along the longitudinal and lateral axes during peak acceleration.Mass Fraction Sensitivity Analysis: Characterize the structural efficiency by evaluating the structural mass fraction:\(\epsilon =\frac{m_{structural}}{m_{structural}+m_{propellant}}\)Minimize ε by leveraging high-modulus materials and pressure-stabilized tank architectures to maximize payload capability for a fixed gross liftoff mass (GLOM).Phase 2: High-Energy Chemical Propulsion and AerothermodynamicsDesign a liquid-propellant closed-cycle or open-cycle gas-generator rocket engine. For this derivation, assume a cryogenic liquid oxygen (LOX) and refined rocket propellant (RP-1) bipropellant system.       [LOX Tank]             [RP-1 Tank]
           │                       │
           ▼                       ▼
     [Cryo Pump]             [Fuel Pump]
           │                       │
           ├───[Gas Generator]◄────┤
           │          │            │
           │          ▼            │
           │     [Turbine]         │
           │          │            │
           ▼          ▼            ▼
     [Main Injector Face] ◄────────┘
           │
           ▼
     [Combustion Chamber] (P_c, T_c)
           │
           ▼
     [Convergent Nozzle]  (Mach 1 at Throat)
           │
           ▼
     [Divergent Bell]     (Supersonic Expansion to P_e)
Chamber Gas Dynamics: Determine the adiabatic flame temperature (\(T_{c}\)) and mean molecular weight (γ) of the combustion products by executing a chemical equilibrium composition analysis (e.g., NASA CEA) at a specified chamber pressure (\(P_{c}\)) and mixture ratio (O/F).Nozzle Topology and Gas Expansion: Apply the De Laval nozzle isentropic flow relations to map the expansion profile through the convergent-divergent geometry:\(\frac{A}{A^{*}}=\frac{1}{M}\left[\frac{2}{\gamma +1}\left(1+\frac{\gamma -1}{2}M^{2}\right)\right]^{\frac{\gamma +1}{2(\gamma -1)}}\)Where \(A^{*}\) is the sonic throat area and M is the local Mach number. The exit pressure (\(P_{e}\)) must balance the ambient atmospheric pressure (\(P_{a}\)) at the optimum design altitude to minimize over-expanded shock diamonds or under-expanded plume dissipation, maximizing the thrust coefficient (\(C_{f}\)):\(C_{f}=\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma ^{2}}{\gamma -1}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma +1}\right)^{\frac{\gamma +1}{\gamma -1}}\left[1-\left(\frac{P_{e}}{P_{c}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma -1}{\gamma }}\right]}+\frac{P_{e}-P_{a}}{P_{c}}\frac{A_{e}}{A^{*}}\)Transient Heat Flux and Regenerative Cooling: Manage the extreme heat flux (q) transferring into the chamber walls via the Bartz Equation for convective heat transfer coefficients:\(h_{g}=\left[\frac{0.026}{D_{*}^{0.2}}\left(\frac{\mu ^{0.2}C_{p}}{Pr^{0.6}}\right)_{c}\left(\frac{P_{c}}{C^{*}}\right)^{0.8}\left(\frac{D^{*}}{D}\right)^{1.8}\right]\cdot \sigma \)Route the fuel through milled copper-alloy cooling channels (e.g., Narloy-Z) lined with a thermal barrier coating (TBC) to keep the sub-scale material structural temperatures below the yield point.Phase 3: Elastodynamics, Aeroelasticity, and Structural MechanicsThe airframe must withstand combined asymmetric aero-mechanical loads while maintaining rigid structural margins under compression, bending, and internal pressurization.Aeroelastic Stability and Flutter: Compute the vehicle's structural modes to ensure no coupling between the aerodynamic forces and the elastic deformations of the thin-walled cylindrical shell. The primary failure mode to mitigate is panel flutter and local buckling under aerodynamic shear, governed by the Von Kármán plate equations modified for supersonic potential flow.Aerodynamic Center and Static Margin: Model the vehicle's aerodynamic coefficients across the transonic, supersonic, and hypersonic regimes. Ensure the static margin (S.M.) remains positive throughout atmospheric transit:\(S.M.=\frac{X_{CP}-X_{CG}}{D_{r}ef}\)Where \(X_{CP}\) is the center of pressure derived from the integrated normal force distribution, \(X_{CG}\) is the time-varying center of mass due to propellant depletion, and \(D_{ref}\) is the core stage diameter.Pogo Oscillation Attenuation: Mitigate the structural-propulsion closed-loop instability known as the pogo effect. Model the longitudinal structural vibration modes of the airframe alongside the hydraulic inertance and compliance of the propellant feedlines. Integrate gas-charged pogo accumulators to decouple the fluid resonance from the primary structural frequencies.Phase 4: Guidance, Navigation, Control (GNC), and Avionics ArchitectureThe avionics system must maintain attitude control and execute precise trajectory tracking under highly non-linear, time-varying aerodynamic and inertial conditions.State Estimation via Sensor Fusion: Implement an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) or an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) to fuse high-frequency IMU accelerometer and gyroscope data with low-frequency GNSS and star tracker updates. The continuous-time system state model is formalized as:\(\.{x}(t)=f(x(t),u(t))+w(t)\)Where x is the 12-state kinematic vector (position, velocity, attitude quaternion, angular velocity), u is the control input, and w is zero-mean Gaussian process noise.Attitude Control and Thrust Vector Actuation: Actuate the gimbaled rocket engine using hydraulic or electromechanical actuators. Derive the control laws using a Robust \(H_{\infty }\) or Linear-Quadratic Regulator (LQR) framework to govern the state-feedback matrix K, minimizing the quadratic performance index:\(J=\int _{0}^{\infty }\left(x^{T}Qx+u^{T}Ru\right)dt\)The controller must dynamically counteract aerodynamic overturning moments, slosh dynamics within the partially empty propellant tanks, and asymmetric thrust misalignments.Real-Time Trajectory Optimization: Deploy a closed-loop guidance algorithm, such as Powered Explicit Guidance (PEG) or convex-optimized sequential programming, on the radiation-hardened flight computers to continuously re-compute the optimal thrust pointing vector (\(\vec{1}_{u}\)) required to achieve the target orbital insertion parameters at engine cutoff (SECO).Phase 5: Verification, Validation, and Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) TestingBefore clearing the vehicle for flight configuration, it must pass a rigorous matrix of empirical verification protocols.Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) Simulation: Connect the flight computer hardware to a real-time simulator running a 6-DOF (Degrees of Freedom) physics engine. Inject synthetic sensor data to simulate anomalous flight conditions—such as actuator saturation, sensor drift, and severe wind shear profiles—to validate the fault detection, isolation, and recovery (FDIR) software loops.Static Fire and Dynamic Structural Testing: Subject the fully integrated stage to modal testing (shaker tables) to verify the analytical finite element models (FEM). Conclude with a full-duration static fire test on a highly instrumented vertical test stand equipped with high-frequency piezoelectric pressure transducers and cryogenic flow meters to verify the steady-state and transient performance of the turbomachinery.To tailor this engineering architecture to a specific mission profile, could you provide details on the targeted specific orbital insertion parameters (e.g., apogee, perigee, inclination), the preferred machining and manufacturing tolerances available for the turbomachinery impellers, or the computational throughput limitations of your rad-hardened flight hardware?

Those who are wondering about the flash at the end: it was most likely an external flash used for high-speed/slow-motion recording, probably around 1000 FPS.
At that speed, normal lighting isn’t enough for the camera to capture sufficient detail during such an extremely short exposure. A very powerful light source is used to illuminate the scene. So no, the cube didn’t spark. it was the lighting setup for the high-speed camera.

snippet.textDisplay:
Honestly, this summarizes my feelings about a lot of "generative" ai tools. Sure, the machine does it faster than a human, and similar technologies are genuinely useful to us in other contexts (manufacturing, etc.)

But Rubix cubes are fun to solve. These solving machines are nothing but a cool experiment because people genuinely enjoy the process. When the process matters as much as (if not more than) the result, AI can never truly replace human thought and effort. 

Because the final cube isn't what matters. It's the process of solving it.

snippet.textDisplay: For those who didn't understand: Air is one of the most essential and fascinating elements of our planet, even though it is invisible and often taken for granted. It is a mixture of gases that makes up the Earth’s atmosphere, surrounding us completely and protecting life in countless ways. The composition of air is mainly nitrogen (about 78%), oxygen (about 21%), and a small percentage of other gases, including argon, carbon dioxide, neon, helium, methane, and traces of water vapor. Despite its invisibility, air has weight, takes up space, and is constantly moving, shaping weather, climate, and life on Earth. The Earth’s atmosphere, which is made of air, is divided into several layers. The troposphere is the lowest layer where humans, animals, and plants live. Almost all weather phenomena, like rain, snow, and storms, occur in this layer. Above it is the stratosphere, which contains the ozone layer that protects life by blocking harmful ultraviolet rays from the sun. Higher still are the mesosphere, thermosphere, and exosphere, each with unique characteristics and gradually thinner air. In the higher layers, air becomes so thin that humans cannot breathe without special equipment, yet these layers are important for satellites, radio communication, and protecting Earth from meteors. Air is essential for life in many ways. Oxygen, the gas we breathe, is vital for respiration, the process by which our bodies convert food into energy. Without oxygen, humans and animals could not survive. Plants, on the other hand, rely on carbon dioxide, another component of air, to perform photosynthesis, a process that produces oxygen as a byproduct. This incredible balance between oxygen and carbon dioxide keeps life sustainable on our planet. Even the tiniest organisms, like bacteria and plankton, depend on air to live and contribute to the cycles that make Earth habitable. Air also influences climate and weather. Winds, storms, and hurricanes are caused by the movement of air as it responds to differences in temperature and pressure. The pressure of air, known as atmospheric pressure, changes with altitude and temperature, affecting everything from breathing to the way airplanes fly. Air carries water vapor, dust, pollen, and tiny particles that help form clouds and precipitation. The wind’s movement distributes heat around the planet, making some regions warmer and others cooler. In this way, air is not only life-giving but also a constant force that shapes the environment. Beyond nature, air has countless practical uses in human life. Airplanes rely on the movement of air to lift off and stay in the sky. Wind turbines harness the kinetic energy of moving air to generate electricity. Gases from the air, like oxygen and nitrogen, are used in medicine, industry, and scientific experiments. Even sound travels through air as vibrations, allowing us to communicate, listen to music, and experience the world around us. However, air can also be polluted by harmful gases, smoke, chemicals, and dust, which affect both health and the environment. Breathing polluted air can cause diseases like asthma, lung infections, and even heart problems. Human activities such as driving cars, burning fossil fuels, and deforestation increase air pollution and contribute to climate change. Protecting clean air is therefore crucial not only for human health but also for the survival of countless plants and animals. Air is constantly moving and changing. On calm days, we might not notice it, but even a gentle breeze or a strong wind demonstrates air’s power. It shapes landscapes by eroding rocks, carries seeds to help plants grow in new places, and even influences ocean currents and weather patterns across the globe. Without air, Earth would be silent, lifeless, and barren—a stark contrast to the dynamic, living planet we know. In conclusion, air is invisible but indispensable. It sustains life, shapes weather, regulates climate, enables technology, and connects all living beings on Earth. From the oxygen we breathe to the winds that travel across oceans, from the clouds that bring rain to the protective ozone high above, air is everywhere, dynamic and powerful. Respecting and protecting it is one of the most important responsibilities of humanity because clean, healthy air is truly the foundation of life itself.

snippet.textDisplay:
@brunox123 Digging far to deep into this (was thinking of writing an article, maybe in the future), they would probably want to go for under under 50 milliseconds and pure carbon fiber just wouldn't work. It is more brittle than people realize, hard to work with, and cost prohibitive.

Carbon-fiber reinforced thermoplastics would get you to a certain point but if

Moving to a generative-designed titanium central core. By keeping the core skeletal, the weight is identical to plastic, but the yield strength is boosted by over 1,700%

But at high linear speeds, physical friction can lead to instant surface melting. Wrapping internal sliding tracks with Ultra-High-Molecular-Weight Polyethylene (UHMWPE) or Teflon (PTFE) drops the coefficient of friction to around 0.04. This mitigates dynamic heat build-up without requiring wet lubricants that can coat color-sensing optical systems.

So doing this all to a new cube COULD potentially allow them to go to even quicker speeds, provided they build a bot that could reach those speeds, without destroying the cube.

​@GDubby69 no, he means impact frames. You could have just googled.

'Impact frame' is the term in animation for when an action or impact is exaggerated by adding extra flair. For example two characters are fighting and one lands a good punch, right before and after the frame where the hit connects, the animators might have the background flash a different colour or they may add action lines, bold outlines, whatever, the point is that exaggerated "pop" of action that makes the hit feel more powerful. Watching a Jujutsu Kaisen fight scene might be a good example, as that show uses impact frames a LOT.

​@TodKarlsonNah people who speed solve it inspect it first, even if they do the manipulation blindfolded. There are various algorithms for solving it and the optimum varies depending on the initial state. Often, the quickest solution employs first one algorithm, then another. As for the 43 quintillion states... the restrictions imposed by the fixed relationship between the three facets on each corner and the two on each middle edge piece mean that there are (43 quintillion divided by 12) states.
